Under processes the scan left the live graph alone, but `discover_redaction_zones()` runs in threads on every strategy except worker recycling (#458) and left all four resident there too. The figures were the same on 3.12.14 and 3.14.7t. On a free-threaded build, where threads are the default, that broke "heavy arrays are never kept resident by default" once per scanned instance. Each frame the OCR pass loaded is now released with `unload_pixel_data()` when that instance is done, including when the pass failed after the load. A frame that was resident **before** the scan is left exactly as it was, whether it was an unsaved replacement (#293) or a frame the caller had loaded. What protects the caller's frame is that gate, not the choice of `unload` over `discard`: a frame the scan loaded itself is never an unwritten replacement. The tier-2 `pixel_analysis.analyze_pixels`, and through it `RedactionVerifier.verify_instance`, behave the same way when called directly; a caller who wants the frame afterwards calls `get_pixel_data()`.

- **The OCR docs showed zones that the configuration loader refuses, and a discovery example that stored the wrong object (#424).** `docs/ocr.md`'s Configuration Reference labelled `redaction_zones` entries `[x, y, width, height]`, but zones are `[y1, y2, x1, x2]` everywhere they are read (#258, #264). Its two examples, and the Applying Zones example, were box values that fail validation. Loading either page's YAML as published printed `Load failed: Rule #0 (…), Zone #0: Invalid ROI logic (Start > End).` and left the session with **no rules**, because `load_config()` resets them on a validation error (a separate, pre-existing silence, filed as its own issue). `docs/configuration.md` passed `discover_redaction_zones()`'s `DiscoveryResult` straight to `add_rule(zones=…)`. That stored the object as the rule's zones, which the loader, the verifier and redaction each refuse with a different `TypeError`/`ValueError`, and its print reported the candidate count as a zone count. The pages now use zone space, convert the examples from the boxes they meant (`[20, 50, 200, 30]` becomes `[50, 80, 20, 220]`, which is `to_zones()`'s own output for that box), and take zones as `[z["zone"] for z in result.to_zones()]`. `tests/test_documented_zones_are_zone_space.py` validates every documented zone with the loader's own rule, checks that no zone fence carries a box-space label, and executes the configuration page's example against a real `DiscoveryResult`.
- **The hang probe calls a hang by silence, not by the clock, so a slow suite is no longer reported as a hang (#427).**
  - **What was wrong.** `.github/workflows/hang-probe.yml` declared an iteration `HANG` once it had run for `per_iteration_minutes` (default 15). The input's description said the runner suite takes 5m30–6m. It now takes 721–836 s. In run 34488760203, iteration 2 was killed as `HANG` at 946 s, after pytest had printed `1855 passed, 1 skipped in 899.50s`. Its SIGUSR1 dump shows the main thread in teardown garbage collection (`gc_collect_harder`, called from `pytest_unconfigure`) 0.5 s after the summary. That verdict would have blocked a release. The `iterations` input also promised a "hard ceiling 22", worked out at 15 minutes, and nothing enforced it. At the recommended `per_iteration_minutes=25` the real ceiling was 13, and more iterations than that would run into the 340-minute step cap mid-iteration. That is the "cancelled, no failing step" shape of #243.
  - **What changed.** `HANG` now means no new test has started for `stall_minutes` (a new input, default 10). Progress is the number of test node ids pytest `-v` has printed **at column 0**, counted rather than measured by file size, because the conftest stall watchdog keeps writing through a real hang. Run 34073209412's fork log grew every 120 s for 850 s with one test in flight. The count is anchored because the watchdog names the stuck test indented. A run that has printed its summary and then stays silent for `stall_minutes` is `HANG(exit)`. It still blocks (owner ruling): a process that will not exit is a hang. `per_iteration_minutes` keeps its name, so an existing `-f per_iteration_minutes=N` still dispatches. It is now the ceiling for a run that is still starting tests, default 45 (3.2× the slowest healthy iteration): a test that starts at or after it makes the row `SLOW`. A run that went silent before the ceiling is never `SLOW`. It is judged by `stall_minutes` alone, so an iteration lasts at most the ceiling plus the stall. The first version keyed the ceiling on elapsed time, and the PR's review found what that does: a stall that began less than `stall_minutes` before the ceiling met the ceiling first and read as `SLOW`, a green job. At the documented `per_iteration_minutes=25`, a teardown hang after run 34488760203's summary at 899.5 s would have been `SLOW` at 1500 s, after 600 s of silence. Both minute inputs must be positive whole numbers. GitHub's `type: number` accepts `12.5`, which used to end the script at its first `$(( ))` with no row and no `::error::`, and now fails up front naming the input. The script also carries its own 330-minute budget, inside the step's 340-minute cap. It will not start an iteration that the longest one so far says cannot fit, and it limits a started iteration to what is left, with the kill's grace reserved, silent or not. Either case is a `BUDGET` row. The step cap is a backstop again, whatever the inputs.
  - **Why 10 minutes.** Across the twelve healthy spawn iterations downloaded, the watchdog never reported, so every healthy gap between tests was under 130 s. 600 s is past `faulthandler_timeout` (300 s) and the worker's 240 s dump, so every internal dump has fired before the probe kills. Run 34073209412's real hang would have been called at about 600 s instead of 945 s. `tests/test_packaging_contract.py` pins both of these inequalities against their sources: the stall deadline outlasts every internal timeout, and the ceiling exceeds the stall deadline. That second pin used to be what kept a stall from reading as `SLOW`. Since the review keyed `SLOW` on progress, it is not: a stall is judged by `stall_minutes` at any ceiling. It stays as a floor, because the slowest healthy iteration (about 14 minutes) is above the 10-minute stall, so a ceiling at or below the stall would call every healthy run `SLOW`.
  - **Decision table.** `HANG`, `HANG(exit)` or `LOCKED` blocks the release and reopens #250: `::error::`, the loop stops, the job is red. `SLOW` or `BUDGET` is no verdict: `::warning::`, the loop stops, the job is green, re-dispatch. `failed(rc=N)` is recorded and the loop goes on. Ten `clean` rows is the pass. Every killed iteration gets the same SIGUSR1 dump before the group KILL, so a `SLOW` log says where the time went. The table is also in the workflow's header, because the release runbook that uses it is untracked. Ten iterations now take about 140 minutes.
  - **How it is tested.** Nothing ran the loop script before. `tests/test_hang_probe_loop.py` extracts it from the YAML and substitutes every `${{ }}`. It runs the script under GitHub's own `bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail`, against a fake pytest on `PATH` (with a Python `setsid` shim, since macOS has none), through one scenario per outcome. The scenarios check that USR1 arrives before the KILL, that the KILL reaches a forked grandchild through the process group, that re-enabling `-e` loses the row, that a hang beginning just before the ceiling is still `HANG` or `HANG(exit)`, and that the fake's first line is pytest's real `=`-ruled session banner, so a summary pattern loosened to any ruled line is caught. The script reads five test-only knobs (`PROBE_UNIT_S`, `PROBE_POLL_S`, `PROBE_GRACE_S`, `PROBE_MARGIN_S`, `PROBE_BUDGET_S`) with production defaults. They are unset in CI, and `test_packaging_contract.py` pins every default and checks that no `env:` in the workflow sets them. The file takes about 47 s (45.5–48.7 s over ten runs on each interpreter), all of it on the PR gate's `Run Tests` step, whose own headroom is #475.
- **The mutation probe's per-mutant timeout is derived from the module's own control pass, and a timeout is reported as one (#442).**
  - **What was wrong.** `run()` gave every mutant a flat 900 s, and `main()` caught `TimeoutExpired` in its generic `except` and printed it as `skipped`, outside the tally. A mutant that stopped the tests terminating, in a module whose whole list passes in one second, cost fifteen minutes and was scored as neither killed nor survived. A control that timed out escaped `main()` and ended a multi-hour run.
  - **What changed.** `main()` times the control, and each mutant then gets `max(30 s, 3 × control)` (`mutant_timeout()`). Measured controls give session.py about 929 s, today's value to within 3%, and discovery.py 30 s. A mutant that times out prints `TIMEOUT … (limit Ns)` and counts as detected (owner ruling): the tests noticed by not finishing. The tally reads `killed K/N (T by timeout)`. Any other exception is still `skipped` and still outside `n`. The control runs under a fixed 1800 s. It sets every other limit, so it must not be what a loaded machine times out. If it does, the run prints `TIMEOUT after 1800s -- results unusable` for that module and goes on to the next. `run(tests, timeout)` takes the limit as a required argument, so a default cannot bring the flat value back.
  - **The false reason.** `NOT_PROBED`'s reason for `discovery.py` named the wrong mutant. Flipping `visited = [False] * n` to True fails in 1.5 s at 0e3e38c. The mutant that never terminates is `visited[neighbor] = True` flipped to False: the BFS re-enqueues visited nodes forever, and its RSS grows by about 2 MB/s. It is caught in 2 s today only because the probe's `-x` stops on `test_merge_disjoint` first, on 3.12 and 3.14t alike. The reason now says so. The module is still deferred, since over 20 of its survivors are unclassified (#439).
  - **A timeout takes the whole pytest with it (#476).** `subprocess.run(timeout=)` kills only the direct child, so a mutant spinning inside a `run_parallel()` worker left that worker running after pytest was gone. The review of this PR measured busy spawn workers at about 77% CPU each, reparented to init, inside every later mutant's timing. `run()` now starts pytest with `start_new_session=True` and, on `TimeoutExpired`, sends SIGKILL to that process group before re-raising. The workers inherit the group, and the new session makes it pytest's alone. `tests/test_mutation_probe_timeouts.py` times out a stand-in whose child sleeps past the limit and asserts the child is gone, and it pins that `run()`'s `timeout` has no default.

- **The exported BitsStored is a width the pixel values fit; a declared width they do not fit is rewritten to the array's own, and so is a missing one (#468).** Both public write paths, `session.export()` and `DicomExporter.write_tree()`, share the worker this changes.
  - **The defect.** Measured on 168fdd6, 3.12 and 3.14t. `_export_instance_worker` wrote BitsStored and HighBit from `attributes` when the instance declared them and from a default of 8 (one-byte arrays) or 16 (every other) when it did not, and held neither against the array written beside them. An `int32` array with no declaration left under BitsStored 16, and a reader got 27734 where -1103401898 was written (`uint32`: 65535 where 4294967295). `int16 [-3024, 3000]` under a declared BitsStored 12 was written as declared; every conformant reader masks a native sample to BitsStored, so it read back 1072 and -1096, in one frame of a multi-frame as in a single frame. Under JPEG 2000 the codestream carried the values exactly beneath a header claiming a width they exceed. A declared BitsStored 17 over 16-bit bytes was written too, and pydicom refused to decode the file at all. `verify_readback=True` (#449) failed the first two after the fact; the default export wrote each in silence.
  - **Now.** The width is held against the array (`_stored_width`). With no declaration, `BitsStored = BitsAllocated = itemsize * 8` and `HighBit = BitsStored - 1`. A declared width is written as declared when every sample fits it, checked to the last value at both ends for the array's own signedness (-2048 and 2047 fit 12 signed bits, 4095 fits 12 unsigned; -2049, 2048 and 4096 do not). **When a sample does not fit, or the declaration is above BitsAllocated or below 1, the file gets the array's own width -- a declared descriptor is rewritten -- and the graph is not touched**: `attributes` still says 12, and a second export makes the same decision again. No audit row: nothing was lost and the file is correct, so the grade must not move. The rewrite is logged at INFO, one line per widened instance naming the declared width and the values, on the `isocenter` logger **of the process that called `export()` or `write_tree()`**: the worker hands the sentence back on its `ExportOutcome` (`corrections`, beside `losses`) and the parent logs it (`_report_export_corrections`), only for files that were written. Logged in the worker, as this entry's first cut did, it reached no one: `session.export()` always runs the worker in spawned processes, `write_tree()` does on a GIL build, and a spawned child's `isocenter` logger has no handler (measured in the review of #506: 3 widened instances, 0 lines). The line is pinned through `session.export()` with and without `ISOCENTER_FORCE_THREADS`, and through `write_tree()`, reading the parent's records. **What that allows, stated plainly: a series in which only some slices overflow their declaration comes out with mixed BitsStored**, the declared width on the slices that fit and the array's on the ones that did not. The width written is BitsAllocated and not the narrowest that holds the values, because the narrowest is a property of one frame's content and would do that to every series. The range is the array's `dtype.kind`, not declared PixelRepresentation; a declaration that contradicts the bytes is the separate defect filed as #499. Cost: one min/max pass per instance whose declaration is narrower than its bytes, 4 ms on a 52 MB int16 stack beside the 4 ms `tobytes()`.
  - **HighBit follows BitsStored.** HighBit is written as BitsStored − 1 wherever BitsStored is written, never as declared: the array holds right-aligned values, so its most significant stored bit is BitsStored − 1 whatever the source said. A kept declaration with an inconsistent HighBit therefore goes to disk coherent: 12/15 is written as 12/11, and 16/11 as 16/15. **A byte change the first cut of this entry did not state:** a HighBit declared with no BitsStored beside it (11, say) used to be written as BitsAllocated 16, BitsStored 16, HighBit 11, and is now written as 16/16/15.
  - **A malformed BitsStored is no declaration.** The declared value is read by `declared_int`, the reading the geometry descriptors and `set_pixel_data()` already get, so absent, `''`, unparseable and non-scalar values all mean not declared, and get the array's own width with nothing logged. That includes a one-element list. `[12]` was exported as 16/12/15 before this change, because pydicom unwraps it, and the first cut of this change failed it with `TypeError: int() argument must be a string, a bytes-like object or a real number, not 'list'` (review of #506). It is now written as 16/16/15, as a list-valued Rows is read as not declared, rather than by a second, more lenient rule for one descriptor. A numeric string (`"12"`) is still a declared 12. `''`, which failed the readback before this change, is pinned beside `[12]`.
  - **Reach.** Not an ingested file re-exported as it came: a native source's decode is already masked, so it fits. It is reached from `set_pixel_data()`, which writes BitsAllocated and PixelRepresentation from the array but not BitsStored, so replacing an ingested 12-bit CT's pixels with wider values left the old width beside them; from a J2K source whose codestream was wider than its header; and from a hand-built graph. Pinned in `tests/test_export_bits_stored.py` at both paths, both syntaxes, int8/uint8/int16/uint16/int32/uint32 and bool, at the bound and one past it. `tests/test_export_readback.py::test_values_outside_bits_stored_fail_an_uncompressed_readback` now writes its overflowing file by hand and holds `_verify_readback` against it directly, since the worker no longer produces that file; the readback's own masking claim is unchanged.

- **A 3-sample array declared `YBR_FULL_422` is exported as `YBR_FULL`, on both transfer syntaxes (#470).** `YBR_FULL_422` names a layout -- two chroma samples per two pixels, four bytes per pair -- that the graph cannot hold: the array is `(rows, cols, 3)`, and `tobytes()` of it is a third longer than the label promises.
  - **The defect.** Measured on 168fdd6, 3.12 and 3.14t: an 8-bit 8x8x3 instance labelled `YBR_FULL_422`, exported with `use_compression=False`, was written with its full-resolution samples under the subsampled label, and pydicom refused the file: `ValueError: The number of bytes of pixel data is a third larger than expected (192 vs 128 bytes) ...`. The same for two frames, odd columns and 16-bit samples. Under JPEG 2000 the file decoded, beneath a label the codestream contradicts. `verify_readback=True` failed the native case (`could not be decoded (ValueError: ...)`); the default export wrote it in silence.
  - **Now.** `_write_pixel_geometry` writes `YBR_FULL` where a 3-sample array is declared `YBR_FULL_422` (compared stripped and upper-cased, as the resolver compares), on the native and the JPEG 2000 path alike, so the same bytes carry the same label under either syntax. It corrects only what the shape proves, the sampling; the colour-space half, YBR, is the declaration's and is kept, because three samples are equally RGB or YBR and a relabel to RGB would be a label without its bytes (#372, #448, #482). One and two samples under the label are not relabelled: one is the resolver's contradiction and comes out MONOCHROME2 as before, two is a shape no interpretation names and is written as declared. The graph keeps its label, and `resolve_photometric_interpretation` and `set_pixel_data()` are untouched -- the `PlanarConfiguration` split (#210, #217): they answer what the graph should carry, the exporter describes the element it just wrote. Reach is hand-built graphs only; ingest relabels every 8-bit YBR source from the decoder's output and refuses 16-bit YBR. Pinned in `tests/test_export_ybr_full_422.py`. The four other YBR labels a native file may not carry (`YBR_PARTIAL_422`, `YBR_PARTIAL_420`, `YBR_ICT`, `YBR_RCT`), which pydicom reads without complaint, are filed as #502.

### Removed

- **`imagecodecs_handler.needs_to_convert_to_RGB` and `should_change_PhotometricInterpretation_to_RGB` (#440).** Both returned `False` unconditionally, and nothing in the package, the tests or the docs called them. They were hooks in pydicom 2.x's pixel-handler interface. pydicom 3, the floor since `pydicom>=3.0.0`, never reads the handler list, and `Instance.get_pixel_data` calls the handler module directly. Their four mutants were permanent survivors in every mutation-probe run of the module. Measured on the branch at stride 1, the row went from 64 sites, 58 killed and six survivors to 60 sites, 58 killed and two survivors (both the equivalent prints the row's comment names). #478 and #464 have since added 19 sites to the module (79 now, still stride 1 at budget 60), and those are not re-measured here. The full suite is green without them. `imagecodecs_handler` is not listed on `docs/api/stability.md`, so it is tier 3 and this is not a breaking change. No test pins their absence: that would pin text, not behaviour. The probe row itself is the guard, because re-adding either function brings back two survivors in every default run's output, and that is how they were found.

## [0.9.5] - 2026-09-10

### Breaking

- **BREAKING: `Session.scan_pixel_content()` and `Session.discover_redaction_zones()` now raise `pixel_analysis.OcrUnavailableError`, a `RuntimeError`, when OCR cannot run, instead of reporting an empty result (#422).** Before any worker is dispatched -- and before either method looks at the graph -- each call checks that `pytesseract` imports **and** that the `tesseract` binary answers `get_tesseract_version()`. If either fails it raises a message naming the method, the reason, `pip install "isocenter[ocr]"` (quoted, because zsh globs the unquoted brackets: `zsh: no matches found: isocenter[ocr]`) and the binary's install command, and says that nothing was scanned. The old behaviour was wrong because the empty result could not be told apart from a clean one. Measured on a six-patient fixture from `scripts/generate_redaction_example.py`: without pytesseract, `scan_pixel_content()` printed `OCR Scan Complete. Found 0 suspicious regions (Uncovered).` for six instances it had not read, and `discover_redaction_zones()` printed `Discovery complete. Found 0 raw candidates.`. With pytesseract installed and no binary on PATH, the same fixture gave 0 findings and 0 candidates behind 60 `OCR failed` log lines, one per frame per pass, where the binary on PATH gives 116 and 126. `HAS_OCR` existed and neither method read it. `scan_pixel_content` is a frozen method whose only job is to catch burned-in text the zones missed, so a silent zero is the worst answer it can give. The check sits first rather than just before the pool because a scaffolded config (a rule with `redaction_zones: []`) would otherwise have `scan_pixel_content()` answer "No matching configured instances" without OCR, and the missing extra would surface only once the zones were filled in. A binary too old for pytesseract to parse is a refusal too: pytesseract signals it with `SystemExit`, which would otherwise exit the caller's script from inside a scan. The return shapes are unchanged: a "not scanned" field on `PhiReport`/`DiscoveryResult` was rejected because it grows two frozen shapes and stays silent for any caller who does not read it. **What the check does not cover:** it is made in the calling process, once per call, so a frame whose OCR fails after it passes is still logged and not reported. Measured in review, with the binary reachable from the parent only (`tesseract_cmd` set there) and processes forced: 0 findings behind 30 `OCR failed` lines, because each spawned worker re-imports pytesseract with its default `tesseract_cmd`. That is #423, and an empty report is not yet proof that every frame was read. `OcrUnavailableError` is tier 2 and not in `isocenter.__all__`; the frozen promise, in `docs/api/stability.md`'s Exceptions paragraph, is `RuntimeError`. `HAS_OCR` still means only "pytesseract imported", and the README, `docs/installation.md` and `docs/ocr.md` now say it does not cover the binary.
- **The import-time `pytesseract not installed` warning is removed (#422).** It was the only sign OCR was missing, and it fired where OCR is never used: once on `from isocenter import Session`, then again in every spawned worker (six each during `ingest()`, `scan_pixel_content()` and `redact()` on the fixture above), while the thread-pooled `discover_redaction_zones()` -- which does use OCR -- printed nothing. The reason now travels in the exception, including the text of the `ImportError`, so a broken dependency of pytesseract reads differently from its absence.
- The tier-2 functions `pixel_analysis.analyze_pixels`, `pixel_analysis.detect_text_regions` and `RedactionVerifier.verify_instance` still return `[]` without OCR -- they run per instance inside workers, where raising would turn one precondition into N worker failures -- and their docstrings now say that `[]` there is not "no text" (#422).
- **BREAKING: `session.export(folder, format="wfdb", ...)` now raises `TypeError` for an option name it does not recognise, where it previously ignored it (#410).** The wfdb exporter read `options.get("patient_ids")` and `options.get("include_annotation_text")` and never looked at the rest of the dict, so `export(folder, format="wfdb", patient_id=["WFPAT-A"])` -- one character off the frozen name -- **exported every patient**, with nothing in the returned list of paths, the log, the audit table or the compliance report saying the subset filter had been dropped. Measured on a two-patient store: the correct spelling wrote `['WFPAT-A_1_0.hea']` and the typo wrote `['WFPAT-A_1_0.hea', 'WFPAT-B_1_0.hea']`, as did a name that was not an option at all. The same typo on `format="dicom"` has always raised, because `_export_dicom` has a real signature and an unknown keyword hits it -- so a de-identification library was loud about a typo on one format and shipped the whole cohort on the other, which has the strictness exactly backwards. **The exact exception**: `TypeError: export(format='wfdb') got unexpected keyword argument(s) 'patient_id'; the wfdb options are 'include_annotation_text', 'patient_ids'.` It is raised as the first statement of `WfdbExporter.export`, before `patient_ids` is read and before any file is written, because a refusal that fires after the walk arrives with the cohort already on disk. `TypeError` and not `ValueError` because it is what Python raises for an unexpected keyword and what the `dicom` path already raised for this mistake; the point of the issue is that the two formats agree. **What breaks:** a caller forwarding one options dict to both formats -- `for fmt in ("dicom", "wfdb"): session.export(out / fmt, format=fmt, **opts)` -- now raises on the wfdb pass for any `dicom`-only option (`use_compression`, `check_burned_in`, `check_reversibility`, `show_progress`, `subset`, `verify_readback`). Split the dict per format; the two formats never honoured the same options, and the loop only appeared to work because one of them was silent. **The measured cost of the strictness:** exactly **one** site in this repository relied on the shrug -- `tests/test_wfdb_writer.py` passing `show_progress=False` for its own convenience -- and it is deleted in the same change. `patient_ids` and `include_annotation_text` remain the two wfdb options, unchanged, and are now the module-level `_WFDB_OPTIONS`, the only place in that module the pair is spelled. **Why 0.9.5 and not later:** `docs/api/stability.md` freezes `export`'s documented behaviour for every 1.x, so this is the last release in which an unknown option can be tightened at all -- loosening a raise afterwards is a patch, tightening a warning afterwards is a 2.0. What an unrecognised option does was undocumented until now, which is what made it a defect rather than a promise; that page now says it. **A freeze pin that could not see what it froze:** `tests/test_wfdb_privacy.py`'s AST pin collects the literal keys the exporter's body *touches* by five syntactic forms, and a name sitting in an allow-list constant is none of them -- measured, a third name in `_WFDB_OPTIONS` left it green. `tests/test_wfdb_option_strictness.py` pins the constant itself, so one test covers what is read and the other what is admitted, and they go red against each other. Not fixed here and filed: the `dicom` path's message still names `DicomSession._export_dicom()`, a tier-3 private method surfaced through a tier-1 public call.
- **A dtype-only `set_pixel_data()` is no longer written off by the frame dedup, and a float instance whose pixels were replaced with integers now refuses the compressed export instead of writing a float file (#406).** `SidecarPixelLoader` snapshots rows, columns, samples, frames, BitsAllocated, PixelRepresentation and the `_ISOCENTER_PIXEL_DTYPE` carrier at construction and rebuilds every frame from that snapshot, and `_persist_pixels`' deduplication arm -- "these exact bytes are already in the sidecar, do not append them again" -- returned the loader's own frame without rebuilding it. So a `set_pixel_data()` that changed only the *type* of the pixels, leaving the bytes bit-identical, hit the dedup and left the loader describing the frame it had replaced. Measured on a `float32` instance handed `floats.view(np.int32)`: the store row, and a reopened session, were right; the live object handed back `float32`; and because the export chooses its pixel container from the array's dtype (`arr.dtype.kind == 'f'`) rather than from `attributes`, `session.export(folder)` wrote a file carrying `FloatPixelData` with float values, beside one `EXPORT` audit row reading `wrote 1 of 1` and no loss row of any kind. The loader is now rebuilt from the live instance when the dedup hits -- **every** field, not just the dtype, because the same window was open on Rows/Columns: a replacement of the same byte length at a new geometry reloaded at the old shape, also measured. **What breaks:** an export of such an instance at the frozen default `use_compression=True` now raises `isocenter.io_handlers.ExportError` (`wrote 0 of 1 planned instances; 1 failed and nothing reached disk`) with an `ERROR` audit row carrying `_J2K_ENCODABLE_FRAMES`' refusal -- `Compression failed: JPEG 2000 lossless cannot carry int32 pixel data at 1 sample(s) per pixel (BitsAllocated 32, PixelRepresentation 1)` -- because the frame is now correctly seen as a 32-bit integer frame, which #404 refuses to compress. It previously "succeeded" by writing the wrong pixels. `use_compression=False` writes the file the caller asked for: `PixelData`, BitsAllocated 32, PixelRepresentation 1, bit-exact. Nothing on the frozen surface moved -- `use_compression` keeps its name and its `True` default; what was promised is the signature, and the promise was never "this always writes a file".
- **`redact()` on a `":memory:"` store now refuses `ISOCENTER_MAX_TASKS_PER_CHILD` instead of failing under it (#400).** 0.9.4's `docs/environment.md` states that with this variable set, `redact()` on a `:memory:` store "runs in processes and fails with `RedactionError` naming `no such table: instance_blobs`". That was accurate, and it was the wrong failure: the pass took the sidecar pass-lock, prepared every task, spawned workers, regenerated a SOP Instance UID per instance, wrote an `ERROR` audit row per failure and a `REDACTION` accounting row per rule-pass, printed a summary, and only then raised -- for a configuration that could have been rejected before any of it, because only `multiprocessing.Pool` implements worker recycling and a spawned worker cannot reach a `:memory:` store at all (`SqliteStore.__setstate__` hands it `_memory_conn=None`, and it opens a fresh, empty in-memory database with no `instance_blobs` table). It now raises **`RuntimeError`** from `redact()` **after** the persistence drain -- so the frozen "`audit()` and `redact()` drain the persistence manager on entry" stays true of a refused call, and a caller who fixes their environment and retries wants that drain to have happened -- and **before** the pass-lock is taken and before any task is prepared: no SOP Instance UID regenerated, no pixel touched, no audit row, no attestation, no console line beyond the refusal. The message names the store, the variable, why processes cannot work for this store, what continuing would have done, and two remedies. **The old failure was never intermittent:** measured on 3.12.14 and 3.14.7t, all three of three instances failed every time, because `execute_redaction_task` ends in `persist_pixel_data` on every task. **A caller who caught `RedactionError`** around `redact()` to handle a partial pass will **not** catch this, deliberately -- nothing was attempted, so the exception meaning "these instances failed" would be the wrong report; `except RuntimeError` does catch it, since `RedactionError` is one. It fires whether or not any image matched, because a configuration that cannot run is refused whether or not it had work to do. `redact_by_machine()` inherits it and its `finally` restores the caller's configuration first. `ISOCENTER_FORCE_PROCESSES` is **not** part of this -- see the `Changed` entry below; the two levers land on opposite sides of one line, and the field that separates them is the resolved `use_threads`, not the lever's name.

- **Every compressed export this project has ever written was non-conformant, and the bytes of all of them change (#404).** Transfer syntax `1.2.840.10008.1.2.4.90`, JPEG 2000 Image Compression (Lossless Only), names a bare **codestream**. Pillow's `Image.save(bio, format="JPEG2000")` with no filename wraps the codestream in a **JP2 box**, and that is what the encapsulated fragment carried: measured on a written file, `codestream head: 0000000c6a5020200d0a870a`, the JP2 signature box, where the standard calls for `ff4f ff51` -- SOC followed by SIZ. Lenient decoders read it anyway, pydicom's included, which is why no release noticed; the project already knew the distinction on the fixture side, since #372 records its J2K fixtures being written `no_jp2=True` "since Pillow's default wraps them in a JP2 box". The new encoder's `codecformat="J2K"` emits the bare codestream, so **the pixel data of every compressed export changes byte-for-byte, including the `uint8` and `uint16` exports that worked** -- the images are identical, the container around each frame is not. A consumer that hashes the encapsulated bytes of a previously exported file will see a different hash; one that decodes the pixels will see the same image. Anything that was reading Isocenter's output was reading a JP2 box under a codestream syntax, and is now reading what the syntax always said it would get. No API changes, no signature changes; this entry exists because a change to the bytes of a released artefact is not something to discover from a diff.
- **`Instance.set_pixel_data()` now raises `ValueError` for a dtype the sidecar cannot round-trip -- `complex64`, `complex128`, `object`, strings, structured and void dtypes, datetimes and `float128` -- instead of accepting it and handing back a different array (#386).** The old behaviour was wrong because nothing anywhere refused these: a `complex64` array recorded no dtype carrier, declared `BitsAllocated 128`, and reloaded through the loader's integer fallback as `uint16` -- silently, with the values wrong. When there was any sign of trouble at all it was a `RuntimeError` from `SidecarPixelLoader` naming a *geometry* mismatch (`Integrity Error: frame for <uid> holds N samples; geometry (4, 4) needs 16`), which sent the reader after the descriptors rather than after the dtype that was never storable. The accepted set is stated **positively**: `dtype.kind in ('u', 'i')` with `itemsize in (1, 2, 4, 8)` -- exactly the domain of the loader's `_INTEGER_DTYPE_BY_BITS`, so the accept rule and the reload table are one statement rather than two that can drift apart -- plus `dtype.kind == 'b'`, plus `dtype.kind == 'f'` whose name is in `SIDECAR_DTYPE_NAMES`. A deny-list would have to be complete to be safe and is wrong the moment numpy adds a kind, silently and in the direction that stores a frame nothing can decode; stated positively, `float128` needs no clause of its own, because it is kind `'f'` and absent from the name set. **Byte order is normalized, not refused**: a big-endian `>i2` is kind `'i'` at 2 bytes and is exactly representable, so it is accepted and stored native-order, and `>i2` and `<i2` now produce byte-identical frames where the big-endian one used to reload byte-swapped. One consequence of that normalization, stated rather than left to be discovered: the stored array is a **copy**, so a caller who mutates a big-endian array in place after the call no longer reaches the frame the instance holds -- the one place where `set_pixel_data`'s own note that "callers mutate arrays in place" stops being true. **The check runs before any mutation.** `set_pixel_data`'s first side effect is `self.pixel_array = array`, so a refusal raised after it would leave an instance describing an array it does not hold -- a new silence inside a fix for silences; the test asserts the surviving *frame* as well as the attributes dict, because only the frame assertion catches a guard moved below that line. The honest limit: this guards the entrance and migrates nothing, so a store already holding an exotic frame is unaffected.

### Fixed

- **Every shipped `pip install isocenter[...]` hint is quoted (#422).** `README.md` (twice) and `docs/ocr.md` (the `ocr` and `nlp` extras) gave the unquoted form, which zsh -- the macOS default shell -- rejects with `zsh: no matches found`. `docs/installation.md` was already quoted.
- **A second `lock_identities()` on the same patient is now the one recovery answers with, and the sequence holds one token instead of a growing pile of them (#399).** `ReversibilityService.embed_identity_token` appended a new item to the Encrypted Attributes Sequence `(0400,0500)` on every call while `recover_original_data` read item **0**, so the *first* capture won forever: locking, remediating, and locking again -- a sequence the documented pipeline does not forbid -- left recovery returning the identity as it stood before the remediation, with the correct capture sitting one index away, decryptable and unread. `lock_identities()` returned a `LockingResult` naming every instance it "modified" on each call, and nothing in the return value, the log, the audit table or the report said that all but one of those captures would never be read. Measured: three locks produced three items; the tail survived `save(sync=True)` and a reopened session on the same database; and `pydicom.dcmread` found all three in the exported file -- so every stale identity a caller ever captured shipped to the recipient, encrypted under the same key as the live one, which is the half of this that is a disclosure question rather than a correctness one. The embed now takes the sequence through `add_sequence()` and replaces its contents (`items[:] = [item]`) rather than appending, **and marks the instance modified explicitly**: `add_sequence()` marks only when it *creates*, so without that line the second and later locks advanced no revision, `has_unsaved_changes` stayed False, the next `save()` skipped the instance, and memory answered with the second capture while the store answered with the first -- a new silence strictly worse than the one being fixed, measured on a re-lock with no other mutation between the two locks. **Not breaking:** no frozen name, parameter or return shape moves, and `recover_original_data` still reads item 0, so a file written by 0.9.4 carrying several items remains recoverable at item 0 -- its old first-wins token. Nothing is migrated, and a single-lock session is bit-identical before and after. **One behaviour is genuinely new:** an instance whose *source* file already carried an Encrypted Attributes Sequence had that foreign item at index 0 and the token appended at index 1, so `recover_original_data` handed the foreign blob to the engine and returned `None` -- such an instance was **not recoverable at all** after a lock, and `recover_patient_identity` printed "No encrypted identity token found or decryption failed" over a token sitting one index away in perfect condition. It is recoverable now, and the foreign item is replaced rather than kept. `items[:] = [item]` rather than `items[0] = item` for that reason: both overwrite the foreign head, because index 0 is where the token goes, so half-preserving its tail would keep the storage and the export cost of a blob nobody can read and reintroduce the ambiguity `recover_original_data` was written not to have. Whether a de-identification library should refuse or report when it overwrites a source element it did not write is filed, not decided here.
- **`imagecodecs_handler` decodes single-frame encapsulated pixel data, which it had never done (#407).** The single-frame arm joined **every** item of the encapsulated `PixelData` and handed the result to `imagecodecs`, and the first item is the Basic Offset Table (PS3.5 A.4) -- four zero bytes ahead of `ff4f ff51` -- so the codec refused every frame with `not a J2K or JP2 data stream`. It failed identically on the JP2 container written before #404, so it is orthogonal to that change and predates it. Only a *populated* offset table breaks the join, which is why nothing noticed: with an empty one the join is accidentally correct, and a hand-built `item(b"") + item(codestream)` fixture passes without this fix. `pydicom.encaps.encapsulate` writes a populated table by default and `_compress_j2k` calls it that way, so every file this project compresses hit it. The frame now comes from `generate_frames`, which the multi-frame arm already used: it skips the offset table and reassembles a frame split across fragments, which "take the last fragment" would not. This makes `Instance.get_pixel_data()`'s imagecodecs fallback work for the population it exists for -- 16-bit multi-sample JPEG 2000, which Pillow cannot decode. It does **not** move `_J2K_ENCODABLE_FRAMES`' `(2, True)` refusal: `ingest_worker` reads through `_decode_pixels` -> `get_decoder(ts).as_array(ds)`, pydicom's own backend, which has no imagecodecs plugin, so `session.ingest()` on such a file still returns `ingested=0` with a `Decompression Failed` row -- measured, and now said in the frozenset's own comment so the guard is not deleted on the strength of the fallback. Giving `_decode_pixels` that fallback is #416.
- **Signed pixel data could not be exported at all (#404).** `session.export(folder)` compresses by **default** -- `_export_dicom(..., use_compression=True)`, an option frozen at `docs/api/stability.md:73` -- and the JPEG 2000 encoder it used accepted exactly `uint8` and `uint16`. So every CT and MR study, which is to say `int16` with `PixelRepresentation 1`, failed with `Compression failed: broken data stream when writing image file`, `wrote 0 of 1 planned instances`, and nothing on disk. **The axis is signedness, not width**: measured one array per dtype against Pillow 12.3.0, `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, `uint32`, `float32` and `bool` all raise that same `OSError`, while `uint64`/`int64` raise `TypeError: Cannot handle this data type` inside `Image.fromarray`. The same data with `use_compression=False` was bit-exact from the same store, which is what settles that neither the sidecar nor the loader was implicated -- the array reaching the exporter was already correct and died at the encoder. The `ERROR` row carried Pillow's own sentence and named neither the dtype, nor `BitsAllocated`, nor `PixelRepresentation`, nor the encoder, nor a remedy; a reader was told a data stream broke. **Why the whole suite was green while this was true**: `tests/conftest.py`'s shared `dummy_pixel_array_2d` was `np.zeros((512, 512), dtype=np.uint16)` -- one of the exactly two dtypes that worked -- and it is `int16` as of this release. `export(verify_readback=True)` could not have caught it either: `_READBACK_DESCRIPTORS` is `("Rows", "Columns", "SamplesPerPixel", "NumberOfFrames", "BitsAllocated")`, it does not include `PixelRepresentation`, and `_verify_readback` never decodes pixels.
- **The encoder is now `imagecodecs.jpeg2k_encode(frame, level=0, codecformat="J2K")`, which is not a new dependency (#404).** `imagecodecs` was already in `install_requires` and already drove the **decode** side in `imagecodecs_handler.py`, so the project already trusted it with pixel fidelity in the other direction. `level=0` is lossless -- measured reversible on a full-range `int16` frame and identical to the explicit `reversible=True`. Supported and measured bit-exact end to end (encode, encapsulate, `save_as`, `dcmread`, compare): **8-bit at any number of samples per pixel, 16-bit at one sample**, signed or unsigned, plus `bool`, which is encoded as `uint8` because the codec refuses kind `b` and because `BitsAllocated 8, PixelRepresentation 0` is what such a frame already declares and what the uncompressed path already writes. That is wider than Pillow's `uint8` and `uint16` greyscale in two directions, not one: `int8`, `int16` and `int8` multi-sample all failed before and all round-trip now. **The import is unguarded, at module scope**, deliberately: a guarded import whose absence turns into `Compression failed` is the same shape as a loader returning `[]` for a missing shipped resource, and this release removes that shape rather than adding one -- `python-dotenv` is the precedent. Consequence: `import isocenter` now fails on an installation missing `imagecodecs`, which is an installation `pip` cannot produce. Pillow stays in `install_requires`, because `pixel_analysis.py` still imports it; `io_handlers.py` no longer does. **One encoder, not two** -- a dual path keeping Pillow for the two dtypes it handled would leave two encoders whose output can diverge for the same input, invisibly, since both produce readable files.
- **`setup.py`'s `imagecodecs` floor is raised from `>=2023.9.18` to `>=2024.6.1`, and the old floor was unbackable in two independent ways (#404).** It publishes no cp312 wheel, so on this project's own Python floor `pip install imagecodecs==2023.9.18` fails outright -- measured: `No matching distribution found` under `--only-binary`, and a failed source build without it. And the encoder now depends on it: the floor has to be a release where `jpeg2k_encode(arr, level=0, codecformat="J2K")` is bit-exact for the supported set. `2024.6.1` is the first release after the old floor, installs from a wheel on 3.12, and was measured exact for `uint8`, `int8`, `uint16`, `int16` and `uint8` RGB, refusing 64-bit, float and bool and encoding 32-bit inexactly -- the same verdicts as 2026.8.16, on which the rest of this work was measured. A bound we cannot back with a passing measurement is a bound we should not keep, which is the same rule the `pydicom<4.0` cap is held to.
- **The compressed path refuses, by name, every frame it cannot write *and read back*: 32- and 64-bit at any shape, and 16-bit multi-sample (#404).** **Exact exception**: `RuntimeError` (an internal `RuntimeError` subclass, so every existing caller is unaffected) reading `Compression failed: JPEG 2000 lossless cannot carry <dtype> pixel data at <n> sample(s) per pixel (BitsAllocated <n>, PixelRepresentation <n>). Here <reason>. Export this study with use_compression=False, which writes the same pixels uncompressed and bit-exact.` The guard is **positive** -- encode only the cells measured to survive a full round trip, `(itemsize, samples > 1)` in `{(1, False), (1, True), (2, False)}` -- because neither the codec's refusals nor its exactness marks the boundary of what is safe to write, and two separate cells prove it. For **32-bit** the codec does not refuse: it **encodes**, exactly to 25 bits and wrong above that, and the DICOM file built from a 32-bit codestream then raises `RuntimeError: Unable to decode as exceptions were raised by all available plugins` on read. For **16-bit multi-sample** the codestream is *exact* and the decoder is what does not exist: Pillow is the only JPEG 2000 decoding plugin this project installs and it reports `Pillow cannot decode 16-bit multi-sample data correctly`, so the library could not re-ingest its own output. That second cell is reachable **only because of this release's own encoder swap** -- Pillow refused a `uint16` RGB frame at `Image.fromarray`, loudly -- so a width-only guard would have replaced one loud failure with `wrote 1 of 1 planned instances` beside a file this library cannot read back (other decoders can -- see the reason clause below). The reason clause is selected by the cell refused, deliberately: telling a user their 16-bit colour pixels are too wide for the encoder would be false and would send them after the wrong thing. The refusal is raised before any encode and before any mutation of the dataset, and is re-raised unwrapped so the sentence is not `Compression failed: Compression failed: ...`. The exception type, the resulting `ExportError`, the `wrote 0 of N` and the empty output directory are all exactly what the default path already produced for those frames, so **this is not a change to what `use_compression=True` promises**; only the speech improves. Falling back to an uncompressed write plus an audit row was considered and rejected: it changes what a frozen option means, and a `DATA_LOSS` row for a fallback that loses nothing would be the kind of false statement this release exists to remove. The set of frames that *do* compress is also **wider** than before: `int8` and `int16` greyscale and `int8` multi-sample all round-trip bit-exactly now and all failed under Pillow.
- **`_compress_j2k`'s reconstruct-from-bytes branch is deleted rather than corrected (#404).** It ran only when `pixel_array is None` *and* `ds.PixelData` existed, and it read those bytes as `uint16` regardless of `PixelRepresentation` -- a silent-corruption sibling of #386 that would have compressed signed data to wrong values without raising. It is unreachable: `_compress_j2k`'s only caller is `_finalize_dataset`, whose only caller is the export worker, which always passes `pixel_array=arr`; and with compression on the worker never assigns `ds.PixelData` at all, which the comment beside that assignment already said. The one path arriving with `arr is None` is the float branch, which has deleted (7fe0,0010) and wants the file written uncompressed. `pixel_array is None` now means "nothing to compress" and nothing else, pinned by a characterization test. Float pixel data is otherwise unaffected and still exports uncompressed per PS3.5 Section 8.2.
- **`set_pixel_data()` recorded a frame's width and never its signedness, so an `int16` array set in memory reloaded as `uint16` and exported as a file declaring `PixelRepresentation 0` beside signed bytes -- measured, `-8` read back as `65528` -- while the audit log said `wrote 1 of 1 planned instances` (#386).** No `DATA_LOSS` row, no `ERROR` row, no warning: the file on disk was internally coherent, decodable, and a different image. **The fix is on the write side and the loader table follows it**, because `_export_instance_worker` writes `ds.PixelRepresentation = inst.attributes.get("0028,0103", 0)` -- fix only the loader and the exported file keeps lying. `set_pixel_data()` now writes `PixelRepresentation (0028,0103)` through `_write_int_if_changed` from the array's dtype kind (1 for `'i'`, 0 for `'u'` and `'b'`), which is the same argument its own comment already makes for `BitsAllocated`: the export writes `arr.tobytes()`, so a descriptor disagreeing with the array cannot be honoured and "the attributes win" was never one of the options. Floats are excluded and **left alone rather than popped** -- PS3.5 Section 8.2 says Bits Stored, High Bit and Pixel Representation shall not be present beside a float pixel element and the export's float arm already deletes all three, so writing a 0 would be a write the export immediately undoes; the stale `PixelRepresentation 1` that survives on an instance given a float array after an int16 one is asserted harmless rather than argued harmless, since the dtype carrier wins on the load path and the exported file carries no Pixel Representation at all.
- **The loader's integer dtype table: `BitsAllocated` {8, 16, 32, 64} crossed with `PixelRepresentation`, replacing `uint16 if bits > 8 else uint8` -- with the old rule kept as the fallback (#386).** Measured before-state, ingesting one 4x4 frame per row and reloading it from the sidecar: `uint8`, `int8`, `uint16` and `int16` round-tripped correctly; `uint32` and `int32` raised `RuntimeError: Integrity Error: frame for <uid> holds 32 samples; geometry (4, 4) needs 16 (one trailing pad byte is tolerated, nothing else)`. That is #373's bound doing exactly what its entry says, on exactly the population that entry names -- the bound was right and the dtype it was checking against was not. **That exception no longer fires for 32- and 64-bit integer frames, and no call that returned now raises.** #373's entry is referenced and deliberately not rewritten: it named this population and cited this issue, and it was right. **The fallback is not tidiness and a table-only rewrite would be a regression**: `BitsAllocated 1` is a real ingested population -- a binary Segmentation, whose packed bits pydicom unpacks to one uint8 per pixel -- and `BitsAllocated 12` arrives as uint16, and neither has a row in the table. Verified by hand-mutation: replacing the fallback with a bare subscript turns both the new one-bit test and the existing `test_export_writes_bits_allocated_the_array_actually_has` red. The same gap existed on the write side -- `set_pixel_data(uint32_array)` raised the identical `RuntimeError` on reload, because the loader had no 32-bit arm whatever put the bytes there -- so one table fix serves both. The rule now lives in one function, `_integer_dtype()`, with **one** caller: `SidecarPixelLoader`. `_compress_j2k`'s reconstruct-from-bytes branch held a third copy of the bucketing that also never read `PixelRepresentation` at all -- a signed frame rebuilt there came back unsigned for exactly the reason the loader's did -- and that branch was first pointed at `_integer_dtype()` here and then **deleted outright** by the #404 entry above, as unreachable from `session.export()` and as a second decoder that could disagree with the loader. So the third copy is gone rather than unified, and this release ships one spelling of the rule and one caller of it.
- **The dtype carrier gains exactly `bool`, and no integer dtype (#386).** `FLOAT_DTYPE_NAMES` is renamed `SIDECAR_DTYPE_NAMES`, because the question it answers is "which dtypes can no DICOM descriptor name", which is wider than "float". numpy `bool_` and `uint8` both declare `BitsAllocated 8` with `PixelRepresentation 0`, so a mask set in memory came back as `uint8` and only its *values* survived -- the same argument #183 makes for float16 and the reason the carrier exists at all. The test asserts the **dtype and not the values**, deliberately: measured, a bool array already round-trips with `np.array_equal` True because `True == 1`, so a values-only test passes on unfixed code and pins nothing. The integers are excluded on the reasoning the #210 comment states -- once `PixelRepresentation` is recorded, `BitsAllocated` and `PixelRepresentation` name every integer dtype the sidecar can hold *exactly*, and a carrier recorded as well would be a second answer to a question the descriptors already answer, and the **authoritative** one, so a graph whose descriptors were later corrected would decode against a stale carrier. Widening the carrier would have regressed the compressed export path, since `Image.fromarray` gives a bool array mode `1`, which Pillow's JPEG 2000 encoder refuses; `_compress_j2k` therefore views a bool frame as `uint8` before encoding -- `view`, not `astype`, because those are the same bytes read under the width the instance already declares.
- **The honest limit on all of the above, in `value_count`'s own direction (#328): a store written by a pre-fix `set_pixel_data(int16_array)` holds int16 bytes beside `0028,0103 = 0`, and still reloads as `uint16`.** Nothing recorded the signedness and no migration can invent it. There is no new stored field and no schema column: the carrier rides `attributes_json` as an underscore key, the channel #183 weighed against a schema change and preferred, and every `SidecarPixelLoader` hydration builds is built with `instance=`, so the carrier and both descriptors arrive together for old and new rows alike. An old row carrying no carrier reaches the extended table and decodes *better* than before -- a 32-bit frame stops raising. NULL is ungraded, not guessed.
- **A missing shipped resource is a broken install, and now says so (#388).** `_load_redaction_knowledge_base`, `_load_ctp_rules` and `ConfigLoader.load_phi_config` each returned an empty collection when a file the package *ships* was absent. Measured, with the resources directory pointed at an empty one: the scaffolded config went from `redaction_zones: [{roi: [50, 100, 50, 200], ...}]` against a real ROI to `redaction_zones: []`, with **zero log lines** at DEBUG on the `Isocenter` logger and **zero audit rows**; the session then ran, redacted nothing by serial, and reported a clean run. `publish.yml`'s own comment says the `phi_tags.json` version "audited against an empty PHI tag list and reported clean". **Exact exception**: `RuntimeError`, raised from all three loaders through one new helper `config_manager.require_package_resource(directory, basename, consequence)`, whose message names the file, the path it looked in, that `setup.py` packages it and `publish.yml` refuses to release a wheel without it, and what continuing would have done -- "scanned every frame with no machine redaction rules", "matched no CTP de-identification rules", "audited against an empty PHI tag list", the last being `publish.yml`'s own wording, so the release gate and the runtime now say the same thing about the same file. So `create_config()` on a broken wheel raises where it previously wrote a config that redacted nothing, and it raises **unwrapped**: no new exception class and no translation layer, because a broken install is not a domain condition and `__all__` stays at five names. **Raise rather than warn**, on #400's ruling, which this reads as one with: a warning in front of a run that then succeeds is a line nobody reads, and there is nothing to annotate, because a missing shipped resource is never a correct state. The degrade-gracefully rule is about the optional extras (`ocr`, `nlp`, `docs`); a shipped package resource is the opposite kind of thing. **Why `RuntimeError` and not `FileNotFoundError`**: `ConfigLoader._load_yaml` already raises that for a *user's* config file, a different failure with a different remedy, and a caller writing `except FileNotFoundError` around `load_config` would silently swallow "your install is broken" -- and, more sharply, the loaders' own handlers are `except (OSError, ...)` and `FileNotFoundError` *is* an `OSError`, so such a refusal drifting inside one of those `try` blocks would be caught and turned straight back into the empty collection, with every test still green. The raise sits before the `try`, and a test kills that pair of edits. **A resource that is present but unreadable or malformed keeps its warning-and-empty-collection**: that is a different failure with a different remedy and is deliberately out of scope, not an oversight. **`ctp_rules.yaml`'s absence is still legitimate and the JSON's is not** -- the YAML is deliberately not shipped and its absence is the ordinary case, so only the JSON fallback goes through the helper. In one line, what a `pip install` from a broken wheel now does that it did not: it raises on the first call that needs the resource, instead of reporting a clean run. Also: `config_manager.RESOURCES_DIR` is now a module-level constant rather than a path computed inside `load_phi_config`'s body, so the arm can be tested at all; and `tests/test_packaging_contract.py`'s docstring and comment, which asserted the old degrade *in prose* while staying green, are corrected in the same change.

- **A zero-item sequence is carried end to end; it used to vanish at ingest with `losses == []` (#392).** A source element saying "this sequence is present and has no items" -- an empty private `SQ` `(0009,1005)` under Explicit VR, or a standard `(0008,1140)` under either transfer syntax -- was absent from the graph after `ingest()`, absent from the exported file, and unmentioned by the session's own accounting: no `DATA_LOSS` row, no `ERROR` row, `IngestSummary(ingested=1, failures=[], declined=0, skipped=0)`, and a single `EXPORT` audit row reading `wrote 1 of 1 planned instances`. Two elements the source asserted were gone and nothing anywhere said so. **The fix is preservation rather than a loss row, and the hop trace is the whole argument.** With an empty `DicomSequence` planted directly in the graph, each of the four hops was measured on its own: (A) source to graph, `process_sequence` -- **dropped**, because the only route in was one `add_sequence_item` per item and zero items made zero calls; (B) graph to `attributes_json`, `_serialize_item` -- **preserved**, measured as `STORED __sequences__: {"0009,1005": [], "0008,1140": []}`; (C) `attributes_json` to graph, `_deserialize_into` -- **dropped**, because `for item_data in items_list` over an empty list never called `add_sequence_item`, measured as `HYDRATED sequences: {}`; (D) graph to file, `_merge_sequences` -- **preserved**, since `ds.add_new(tag, 'SQ', Sequence())` writes an empty `SQ`. Two hops dropped it and two already carried it, so end-to-end preservation costs two one-line edits and **no `DATA_LOSS` row is filed, because nothing is lost** -- #344's own words for the zero-length element it made the same choice about. A fix that preserved the element *and* filed a row would have been a new lie, so `tests/test_empty_sequence_roundtrip.py` asserts the row's absence against a positive control (the `EXPORT` row naming the output folder, read after `flush_audit_queue()`), since an unflushed `SELECT` returns `[]` whether the row is absent or merely late.
- **`DicomItem.add_sequence(tag)` is a new name on the tier-2 entity surface, and `add_sequence_item()` delegates to it.** It canonicalises the tag, creates a `DicomSequence` if there is none, returns it, and calls `mark_modified()` **only when it creates** -- a sequence that newly exists is a change the store must hold, a second call on a tag that already has one is not. Both dropping hops now call it once, before their item loop, unconditionally rather than under an `if not len(elem)` guard, so the empty and the non-empty case are one statement that cannot go stale. One consequence worth knowing before a dirty-count assertion surprises you: **adding the first item to a brand-new sequence now advances `_revision` twice** where it advanced once. That is harmless -- `_revision` is a monotonic counter and `has_unsaved_changes` is a comparison, not arithmetic -- and `test_adding_the_first_item_to_a_new_sequence_still_leaves_one_dirty_entity` states it as a fact rather than a comment, including that a `mark_persisted(revision=captured)` taken before the append still leaves the entity dirty. No exception changes, and no call that returned now raises.
- **The Implicit VR `UN` population is *not* this fix and does not become an `SQ`.** An empty **private** `SQ` under Implicit VR Little Endian never reaches `process_sequence` at all: the transfer syntax carries no VR and the standard dictionary has no entry, so pydicom hands the element over as `UN` with value `None`, it lands in `attributes`, and #344's zero-length arm exports it as a zero-length `UN` -- present in the file, exactly as PS3.5 6.2.2 prescribes for an element whose VR was never known. A **standard** tag under Implicit VR resolves its VR from the dictionary, does reach `process_sequence`, and is covered, which is why the boundary these tests draw is private-versus-standard rather than a property of the transfer syntax. `test_an_implicit_vr_empty_private_sequence_is_still_the_un_population` pins the `UN` behaviour as a characterization test so nobody "extends" the fix into `_sequence_from_un_bytes`. One behaviour genuinely does change downstream: an empty private sequence is now a shape the `remove_private_tags` sweep can see, and it is stripped with the rest of the vendor block (it asks `owner.sequences.keys()` directly since #167 and does not care whether the sequence has items) -- asserted, not assumed.

- **Five pins that could not go red (#396, #397, #401, #394, #383).** Every one of them claimed a fact was checked while nothing checked it, and none was a live user-facing defect. **The frozen output vocabulary** was pinned by grepping `isocenter/` for each word as a quoted literal -- which a docstring, a comment, a SQL string or the logging module's level map all satisfy. Measured: respelling `action_type="WARNING"` at its **only** write site left `tests/test_frozen_surface.py` at `6 passed`. It is now anchored on the write sites themselves by AST, compared for set equality against hand-transcribed literals, so a single-site respelling of a word other sites still spell is red -- the mutant enters the set while the original stays in it. The grep pinned a word only where the package spelled it exactly once, so ten of the eighteen frozen words were unpinned *by that test* -- respellable at every site with it green. (The eight it did pin, and the ten it did not, are listed in the spec's §5.1; the count is reproducible by counting quoted-literal occurrences of each word under `isocenter/`.) This is a narrower claim than "unpinned anywhere": several of the ten are asserted in other test files, which is why the replacement reads write sites rather than counting occurrences. The collector reads `log_audit` in **both** call forms, twenty keyword and one positional, because a keyword-only collector would have left that one site respellable with the pin green. The remaining two of the twenty-three `log_audit` call sites pass a name rather than a literal; both carry `REMEDIATION_*` words, which this page does not freeze. It deliberately cannot see a write *site* deleted while another site spells the word: that is a behavioural change and belongs to the test asserting the row exists.

- **`docs/api/stability.md` named the wrong place to look for 4 of its 13 vocabulary words, and the freeze test could not tell (#396).** The page called all thirteen "the audit `action_type` strings". `REMOVE_TAG`, `REPLACE_TAG` and `SHIFT_DATE` are `PhiRemediation` proposal values reaching a user on the frozen `PhiFinding.remediation_proposal`, and are **never** an audit row -- acting on one writes `REMEDIATION_REPLACE`, `REMEDIATION_SHIFT_DATE` or `REMEDIATION_REMOVE`. `COMPLIANCE_CHECK` is never written to the audit table at all; it is synthesised into the report's `exceptions` list at report time. The page now names five vocabularies -- grade, audit `action_type`, remediation-proposal `action_type`, report exception category, `loss_scope` -- and says which test makes each checkable. **No word joined or left a freeze**; this is a re-categorisation of words already published. The test's single `FROZEN_ACTION_TYPES` list is deleted rather than kept beside the new per-vocabulary names, because two lists claiming the same thing is how the page and the test got out of step.

- **The `wfdb` export option `patient_ids` was frozen on the page and pinned by nothing, and the subset filter behind it had never been exercised (#397).** No test in the repo passed `patient_ids=` to the wfdb path; all thirty `format="wfdb"` call sites exported everything. Measured, both of these were green across `tests/test_wfdb_*.py`, `tests/test_murmur_annotations.py` and `tests/test_frozen_surface.py`: reading the option under a misspelled key, and inverting the membership test so the filter keeps exactly the wrong patient. The second is why a behavioural test was written beside the AST one -- an option name can be right while the filter is inverted -- and it matters because a filter that silently stopped filtering would export every patient's waveforms to a caller who asked for one. The other frozen option, `include_annotation_text`, was already pinned behaviourally and needed nothing. **The issue's suggested fix does not work and was not used:** `WfdbExporter.export(self, session, folder, **options)` reads with `options.get(...)`, so an unknown option is silently ignored and there is no `TypeError` to assert and no signature to pin. That the `dicom` path raises where the `wfdb` path shrugs is filed as #410.

- **`docs/api/stability.md`'s signature table was parsed with `dict(re.findall(...))`, which keeps the last duplicate (#401).** A second `save` row carrying a wrong signature, inserted *above* the true one, left the page publishing a signature the code does not have, with `tests/test_frozen_surface.py` at `6 passed`. The parse moved into a helper that asserts on the `findall` pairs **before** the dict exists. That position is the entire fix: the natural one-liner `len(rows) == len(FROZEN_SESSION_METHODS)` is green *with* the duplicate present, because `dict()` collapsed the two rows before anything counted them. The check lives in the helper rather than inline so that something other than the real page can exercise it -- deleting it must redden both the new unit test and the page test, and it does. Row *order* stays unpinned: the comparison is a dict and the page claims no order.

- **`Session.scan_pixel_content()`, a frozen tier-1 method, had never dispatched its worker in any test (#394).** `session._verify_worker` sat at 14% line coverage -- its `def` line -- so replacing `results = run_parallel(_verify_worker, worker_items, ...)` with `results = []` was a **green** mutation: "the pool is never dispatched" was indistinguishable from working code. The four skip filters, the worker's empty-instance guard and its use of `equipment` were equally unexercised. **Three of the issue's premises are not true of the code** and were not tested for: `scan_pixel_content` builds no lightweight copy, never calls `_rehydrate_findings`, and writes **no audit rows at all** -- so its suggested "assert the audit rows" would have been `assert rows == []`. Its suggested `ISOCENTER_FORCE_PROCESSES=1` test would also have asserted `0 == 0`: `unittest.mock.patch` does not cross a process boundary and neither gate interpreter has `pytesseract`, so the child returns `[]` before touching pixels -- measured, one finding in threads against zero in processes. Process mode is therefore out of scope and the boundary is carried by an explicit pickle round-trip, which unloads the array first so that what crosses is the sidecar loader a real pass sends rather than an array that proves only that numpy pickles. That `PhiFinding.entity` means a live graph object in threads and a dead unpickled copy in processes is filed as #412.

- **`persistence.py` had no row in `scripts/mutation_probe.py`'s `TARGETS`, so no mutant of the sidecar gate was ever generated (#383).** The probe runs only the tests listed for a module, and this one was not a target: `_hold_sidecar_gate`, `_hold_pass_lock`, `_refuse_while_pass_open`, `_flock_within`, `_SIDECAR_GATE_TIMEOUT_S`, the `:memory:` temp-file ownership flag and `compact_sidecar()` -- the machinery #368 put here -- were invisible to the tool whose job is measuring whether the suite can see a change. The row lists all **42** test files whose text matches `isocenter\.persistence\b`, which is what the existing guard demands the moment the row exists; the issue named eight. Budget 30 matches `io_handlers.py` so the two largest modules are sampled at comparable density (453 sites at stride 15 against 519 at 17), and the row's comment records that it roughly doubles a probe run, because an unexplained doubling is the kind of thing someone later "fixes" by cutting the budget. **Scope:** #383 also asked for CLAUDE.md's coverage table to gain a row; `c925829` untracked that file and deleted the tests that read it, so that half has no home in version control and the issue was narrowed to `TARGETS` alone. Its instruction to move four files out of the `io_handlers.py` row is deliberately not done -- they do not import that module but drive `ingest()`, `redact()` and `compact()` through the facade, which is its code on every one of those paths, and whether they buy kill signal is a question a probe run answers and a grep does not.

### Removed

- **`CLAUDE.md` is no longer tracked, and the five tests that read it are deleted.** The file's only reader is the coding agent that works on this repository; it is not documentation, `mkdocs` never built it, and no docs page linked it. The material a human contributor needs is already published in `docs/architecture.md` (the session facade, the object model, the ten checkpoints, hybrid storage) and `docs/developer_guide.md` (environment, lint, testing, release). What remained was the trap list, which is agent-facing, and a set of second copies of facts that already have a Python home: `scripts/mutation_probe.py`'s `TARGETS`, `TrackedEntity`'s real attributes, and the `entity.mark_modified()` call sites in `remediation.py`. Each of the deleted tests existed only to reconcile a copy with its original, so removing the copy removes the need for the reconciliation. Deleted: `tests/test_claude_md_api_names.py` entirely (2 tests); `test_source_citations.py::test_claude_md_cites_every_mark_modified_call_in_the_checkable_grammar`; `test_mutation_probe_targets.py::test_the_claude_md_mapping_matches_targets`; and `test_mutation_runbook.py::test_the_hand_run_subsection_exists_and_names_both_traps`. **No behaviour is left unguarded.** The five `entity.mark_modified()` calls stay pinned by the five reload tests in `tests/test_remediation_invariants.py`, which assert the behaviour and never read a document; `TARGETS` remains the single maintained mapping; and `test_source_citations.py`'s Rule 3 still requires set equality between the line numbers cited in `.py` files and the calls in `remediation.py`, so a sixth call is still red. Measured before and after on 3.14.7: with `CLAUDE.md` absent from a checkout, the suite was **5 failed, 1685 passed, 1 skipped**, every failure a `FileNotFoundError` raised by `pathlib` before any assertion ran; after this change, **1685 passed** with the same 1 skip and no test reads the file.
- **The four `read_text()` calls those tests used had no existence guard, which made the released sdist carry a suite it could not pass.** `MANIFEST.in` grafts `tests/` but never included `CLAUDE.md`, so `pip download --no-binary :all: isocenter && pytest` inside the unpacked 0.9.4 sdist fails those five tests with `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '.../CLAUDE.md'`. Verified against a freshly built sdist: 207 test modules, zero `CLAUDE.md`. The bug predates this change and is fixed by it -- the reads are gone rather than guarded, because a `skipif` would have kept the sdist shipping five tests that never run and `tests/test_source_citations.py` already records why a silent skip must not stand in for a pass.

### Changed

- **`redact()` says so when `ISOCENTER_FORCE_PROCESSES` has no effect on it (#400).** On a `":memory:"` store `redact()` asks for threads per call, and that request outranks the variable, so the pass has always run in threads and the variable has always been ignored -- correctly, since a spawned worker cannot reach an in-memory database. Nothing said so. In a process where `audit()`, `scan_pixel_content()` and `export()` all obeyed the variable, one step did not, and no output mentioned it. That combination now logs one `WARNING` per `redact()` call -- not per `run_parallel` -- naming the store, naming the variable, saying that the request was ignored **and that the run was correct anyway**, saying that the variable still applies to every other parallel pass in the process, and offering a file-backed store for a caller who meant it. It names no knob the reader did not set: `force_threads` appears nowhere in it, because `redact()` set that, not them. **Refusing was considered and rejected**: the result was never wrong, so there is a correct run to annotate, which is #185's case rather than its inverse. The recycling lever is the inverse and refuses -- see the breaking entry above. Nothing warns when both force levers are set (`ISOCENTER_FORCE_THREADS` supersedes by the documented order, so nothing was denied), nor when no lever is set at all (the free-threaded rank is a default, and a default is not a request -- which is what keeps `Session(":memory:")` quiet and working on 3.12, where processes are the default).

- **`redact()` names the execution strategy it resolved (#384).** The console line was `Executing using N workers...` in 0.9.4 and `Executing using N workers (Process Isolation)...` before that; it is now `Executing using N workers (threads)...` or `Executing using N workers (processes)...`, and the parenthetical is read off the `_Strategy` the pool is built from rather than derived a second time at the print site. The 0.9.4 spelling was not false, it was empty: measured across seven store-and-lever combinations on 3.12.14 and 3.14.7t, **three dispatch paths produced one identical sentence**, including the case the issue was filed from -- a file-backed store with no levers set, which runs in processes on 3.12 and in threads on 3.14t. Under threads the worker mutates the live `Instance`; under processes it mutates a pickled copy whose result the parent applies back with `_apply_redaction_outcomes`, so this is the difference that decides what a worker *is*, and it was the one fact the line did not carry. The `INFO` line beside it gains the same field: `Starting granular redaction (N tasks, workers=N, strategy=threads)...`. The recycling `multiprocessing.Pool` reports as `(processes)`, which is what it is; the retired `(Process Isolation)` named an implementation property rather than the choice and left that arm ambiguous. The line says *what*, never *why* -- the why is what #400's warning and refusal are for, and they say it only when it matters. Console `print` lines are tier 2, so this is changeable later with an entry naming both spellings.

- **The #185 worker-recycling warning is emitted at dispatch rather than while the strategy is resolved (#400).** Its text and its frequency are unchanged: one warning per `run_parallel` call whose threads request lost to `maxtasksperchild`, from every entry point including a strategy handed in as `strategy=`. What changed is the one case the move is for -- `redact()` now resolves a strategy *before* deciding whether to run at all, and a strategy that is resolved and then refused says nothing. Without the move, a `":memory:"` store with `ISOCENTER_MAX_TASKS_PER_CHILD` set would have logged `... so this run uses processes.` one line above a refusal of a run that never starts.

- **A malformed parallel tuning value is now reported by a `redact()` that matches no images (#384).** `redact()` resolves its `_Strategy` before it prepares tasks, because the console line has to name the strategy the pool was built from rather than guess at it. Three `ISOCENTER_*` reads moved ahead of the `No matching images found for any loaded rules.` early return as a consequence: `ISOCENTER_MAX_WORKERS`, `ISOCENTER_CHUNKSIZE` and `ISOCENTER_MAX_TASKS_PER_CHILD`, each of which warns when its value is below its minimum. Measured on a `":memory:"` store with a rule matching nothing and the value `0`: each emitted no warning in 0.9.4 and emits exactly one now. `ISOCENTER_DISABLE_GC` and `ISOCENTER_SHOW_PROGRESS` moved with them but are read through `_env_is`, which never warns, so nothing observable changed for those. This is more speech and not less -- a value that will be ignored on the next call that does have work is worth hearing about on this one -- but it is a behaviour change on a call that previously said one sentence and now can say two, and 0.9.4's silence there was not a deliberate quiet.

- **`tests/test_mutation_runbook.py` is now `tests/test_mutation_probe_environment.py`.** Its two surviving tests are genuine environment checks -- that `scripts/mutation_probe.run()` really sets `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE` (read out of `run()`'s source, not asserted as a string), and that a path on `PYTHONPATH` really beats the editable install here, which holds only because this install *appends* its finder to `sys.meta_path` -- and neither ever read a document. The old name and module docstring filed them under a markdown section, which is what made them look like documentation tests.
