  **The honest cost of accepting it is stated in the docstring rather than left implicit**: the error arrives at a *distance* -- at export or verify time, not at compaction time -- and `compact()` reports success, with nothing tying the two together. That is the same distance #153 and #250 were both about, and an owner who weighs it more heavily should take #368 sooner rather than later.

  **The test is a characterization test and says so, and it was verified to be about the failure *mode*, not just the failure.** It is green as written, which is what a characterization test is. Its teeth were measured by mutation, per CLAUDE.md's hand-run recipe: with the hash comparison disabled in `SidecarPixelLoader.__call__` and in `SidecarWaveformLoader.read_raw()`, **four of the six go red** -- `AssertionError: the read after the race returned None instead of raising` -- while phases B and D stay green, correctly, because neither depends on a hash (one raises at the writer, the other on a short read). So the file pins exactly the property the decision rests on: drop `_pixel_hash` from the loader and this window silently becomes wrong pixels, and these tests are where that is caught rather than discovered.

  **Deliberately untouched: #366** (`SidecarManager._lock` is documented by three comments and acquired by nothing; `compact_sidecar` rebinds `self.sidecar`, which is harmless today only *because* that lock is unused). Its two halves have to move together and neither is in scope here.

- **Relicensed from AGPL-3.0-or-later to Apache-2.0 (#348).** `LICENSE` now carries the Apache License 2.0 text and a `NOTICE` file carries the copyright line; `setup.py` declares `license="Apache-2.0"` with the matching classifier; `.zenodo.json` and `CITATION.cff` name the same license, and `tests/test_packaging_contract.py` and `tests/test_version_contract.py` hold all of them together.

  **Why.** A library is adopted by being imported, and Isocenter's whole ecosystem is permissive: pydicom, numpy, pandas, pillow, imagecodecs, PyYAML, pyarrow, cryptography, tqdm and python-dotenv are every one of them MIT, BSD, or Apache. Under AGPL a project that imported Isocenter into an MIT codebase arguably took on AGPL terms, institutional legal review flagged it by default, and a vendor could not embed it at all. AGPL earns that cost as the open half of a dual-licensing model, and there is none. Apache-2.0 over MIT for the explicit patent grant, which is the clause institutional reviewers look for.

  **What is not retroactive.** Releases up to and including 0.9.2 were published under AGPL-3.0-or-later and remain available under it; a relicense changes what future releases grant, not what past ones did. The maintainer is the sole copyright holder (every source commit in the history; the empty-identity commits are MkDocs deploys on `gh-pages`), so no third-party consent was required.

- **The save walk's `prepared` map is keyed on the instance, not on `id(inst)` (#300).** Four sites in `persistence.py` -- the write in `_prepare_pixel_frames`, the read and the membership test in `_save_unsaved_instances`, the read in `_build_instance_writes` -- and the two `Dict[int, ...]` annotations become `Dict[Instance, ...]`. **No behaviour change**: for as long as the graph is alive, which it is for the whole of `save_all`, `prepared[inst]` and `prepared[id(inst)]` select exactly the same instances.

  **Why the map was keyed on `id()` at all.** #287's prepass needed a key that survives the gap between the sidecar writes and the transaction. Three arguments were made for object identity: position cannot (`series_pk` is unknowable before the transaction and a series can be re-parented in between), the SOP Instance UID cannot (redaction mutates it in place, and #288 showed a UID-keyed map is data loss -- the renamed instance is skipped and `_delete_removed_instances` reaps its old row), and the entities were `eq=True` dataclasses, unhashable and value-comparing, so the instance itself could not be a dict key. #299 removed the third argument by making every `TrackedEntity` subclass `eq=False`. The first two stand and are still in the docstring.

  **Why the object key rather than trimming the docstring.** The `id()` spelling needed a liveness caveat -- "`patients` holds the entire graph alive for the whole of `save_all`, so no id can be recycled underneath it" -- that nothing tested and that a future `save_all` refactor could falsify without a red test. An object key holds its own reference, so the caveat is deleted rather than maintained. And `Dict[int, ...]` was the one place in the save walk where an instance was not an instance; the near-miss that motivated #300 was PR #296 prescribing `prepared[inst]` at a moment when it would have raised `TypeError: unhashable type`, which is what happens when a map's key type is not what a reader of the surrounding code expects.

  **The new test is structural, and it says so.** `tests/test_save_all_contract.py::test_the_prepared_map_is_keyed_on_the_instance_itself` calls `_prepare_pixel_frames` directly and asserts `set(prepared) == set(series.instances)` -- set equality, not membership, so a map storing both spellings fails it. It cannot be red on behaviour, because there is none to be red on; it exists so that a reversion to `id()`, or back to the UID, goes through a failing test rather than a paragraph. The behavioural net is unchanged: `test_an_instance_renamed_after_the_prepass_is_still_written` (#288) and `test_an_instance_changed_after_the_prepass_keeps_its_stored_frame` (#274) still pass, and `tests/test_entity_state_vocabulary.py::test_every_tracked_entity_subclass_hashes_by_identity` is what makes the object key safe.

- **The equipment predicate has one spelling: `Equipment.from_parts` (#290).** New public classmethod on `isocenter.Equipment` -- `from_parts(manufacturer, model_name, device_serial_number) -> Optional[Equipment]` -- returning `None` unless a manufacturer or a model name is present. **Four** construction sites now call it, not the three the issue counted: `DicomImporter.import_files`' linkage arm, `SqliteStore.load_all`, `SqliteStore.load_patient`, and `SeriesBuilder.set_equipment`, which had no predicate at all. `tests/test_api_coherence.py` walks the package's AST and asserts no `Equipment(...)` call remains outside `entities.py`, and that `from_parts`' parameters are `dataclasses.fields(Equipment)` in order -- a structural pin, not a second hardcoded list.

  **The measurement that motivated the tests.** With `manufacturer` and `model_name` swapped in the `Equipment(...)` construction at both hydration sites, the full suite was green: 1443 passed. No test read equipment back from the store. #282 had pinned the ingest arm (`tests/test_io.py`), and the two store routes -- the ones every reload of a session goes through -- were unread. `tests/test_persistence.py` gains a partial-equipment test per route, each asserting all three fields on the **loaded** series after `save_all` and a fresh `load_all()` / `load_patient()`, plus a routes-agree test for the serial-only row. Hand-run verdicts, per CLAUDE.md's recipe (`PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, `PYTHONPATH` at the worktree, `isocenter.__file__` printed and read before each run):

  | Mutation | Before refactor | After refactor |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `io_handlers.py` linkage `or -> and` | killed by `test_io` (#282, both rows) | site gone |
  | `persistence.py` `load_all` `or -> and` | killed by the new `load_all` test alone | site gone |
  | `persistence.py` `load_patient` `or -> and` | killed by the new `load_patient` test alone | site gone |
  | `persistence.py` `load_all` argument swap | killed by the new `load_all` test alone | site gone |
  | `persistence.py` `load_patient` argument swap | killed by the new `load_patient` test alone | site gone |
  | `entities.py` `from_parts` `or -> and` | n/a | killed by 10 tests: `test_entities` ×4, `test_persistence` ×4, `test_io` ×2 |
  | `entities.py` `from_parts` `cls(model_name, manufacturer, ...)` | n/a | killed by 11 tests: `test_entities` ×5, `test_persistence` ×4, `test_io` ×2 |

  **Semantics kept, deliberately.** Either identifying field is equipment; a serial alone is not. That is probably the wrong rule -- measured: `Equipment("", "", "SN-ONLY")` on a series is written by `save_all` (the flattened row shows the serial) and comes back `None` from both `load_all` and `load_patient`, so the store keeps the serial and the predicate discards it, while `_match_machine_rule`, the redaction task walk, `_redaction_zones_for`, `services.py` and `verification.py` all key on the serial. A series whose file carries DeviceSerialNumber with an empty Manufacturer (Type 2) and no ManufacturerModelName therefore matches no rule and is skipped by redaction silently. Not widened here: #290 is a behaviour-preserving refactor whose entire proof is "all four routes agree with the ingest rule exactly as it stood", and changing the rule in the same PR removes that proof. The widening is filed separately, and after #290 it is one line in one place, which is what #290 bought. Three characterization tests pin today's rule and name the filed issue; they flip with it.

  **No normalisation.** `Equipment("ACME", None, None)` round-trips through `save_all` and `load_patient` as `Equipment("ACME", None, None)`, so `from_parts` passes `None` through; a test pins that a well-meant `or ""` would change what a reload returns.

  **The one behaviour change, in the builder.** `DicomBuilder...set_equipment("", "", "SN")` previously set an `Equipment("", "", "SN")` that `save_all` wrote faithfully and no reload could return; it now leaves `series.equipment` as `None`. The loss becomes visible at construction rather than at reload. No in-tree caller passes empty identifying fields (`tests/conftest.py`, `tests/test_scaffolding.py`, `tests/test_full_logging.py`, and the three `scripts/generate_*.py` generators all populate all three).

  **Why a classmethod on a frozen dataclass.** "A series has equipment iff it has a manufacturer or a model name" is a statement about what an `Equipment` *is* -- identity is manufacturer and model, the serial is the optional field with the default -- so the rule belongs beside the fields that define it. The constructor cannot express "maybe none": `__post_init__` cannot return a value and a `__new__` returning `None` breaks `dataclasses.replace` and pickling. Rejected: a module-level function (not in `__all__`; a second place to look) and a `Series` method (moves the rule onto the consumer, away from the fields it is about). Positional in field order with all three required, because the constructor is positional, thirty-odd tests call it that way, and every call site holds a serial value -- a default here would be a second spelling of the field's own.

  **`scripts/mutation_probe.py`'s `TARGETS` is unchanged.** The `or` now lives in `entities.py`, which is not a target, and `io_handlers.py`'s probe run no longer sees a site it used to. `tests/test_mutation_probe_targets.py` requires every importing test file to be listed: `entities.py` has 107 importers and `persistence.py` 34, so listing either is a probe-budget decision filed separately. The kill is pinned by the hand-run table above.

### Fixed

- **A lock order documented in three places named a lock nothing ever acquired, and `compact_sidecar` rebound a manager that could not differ from the one it replaced (#366).** Two deletions and three corrected comments. No behaviour changes; `1603 passed` and `pylint 9.37` both unchanged.

  **`SidecarManager._lock` was constructed, excluded from `__getstate__`, recreated in `__setstate__`, and never taken** — not in `write_frame`, not in `read_frame`, not anywhere in `isocenter/`, `tests/` or `scripts/`. Meanwhile three comments documented an order over it: `persistence.py` at the `_pixel_swap_lock` construction and inside `_persist_pixels`, and `session.py` in `_rewire_sidecar_loaders`, the last of which claimed the order was "preserved trivially". A documented invariant with no code behind it is worse than no invariant: it is the shape a reader trusts. All three comments now say what actually serialises writers — `fcntl.flock` on the file inside `write_frame`, which is **cross-process** and therefore not part of any Python lock hierarchy — and note that **`read_frame` takes no lock at all**, which #366's own text and the compaction spec's Q4 both got wrong.

  `__getstate__`/`__setstate__` go with it. They existed only to drop and rebuild the lock; the sole remaining attribute is `filepath`, a string, and default pickling carries it. That matters because the manager pickles into spawned export and redaction workers — verified by round-tripping one.

  **The rebind was inert, and #366's premise that its two halves could not be fixed independently was false.** `compact_sidecar` ended with `self.sidecar = SidecarManager(self.sidecar_path)`. `SidecarManager` holds no mutable state and both `write_frame` and `read_frame` open by path on every call, so the replacement was indistinguishable from the object it replaced — for any writer, holding either one. The issue (and the entry it was drawn from) reasoned that making `_lock` real would turn the rebind into a live bug, so neither could move alone. Measured, that is not the situation: there is nothing to make real, and nothing the rebind changes. Deleted rather than kept, because an assignment that does nothing reads as though it re-points concurrent writers at the compacted file — a guarantee this code does not make and cannot make.

  **What is *not* fixed here, and is the actual defect.** Writers serialise against each other correctly; **compaction is not party to that discipline at all.** It builds `.compact.tmp` and swaps, so it never contends for the writers' `flock`, and a frame appended during the rewrite is committed with a pre-compaction offset into a file the swap discards. That is #368, now re-scoped: the gate is necessary but not sufficient, because a concurrent compaction also destroys an in-flight redaction's frame through the orphan predicate — an exposure interval of a whole redaction pass, which no lock closes. `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-07-sidecar-write-compaction-serialization.md` ships with this change and carries the measurements, including a **reproduced** demonstration that `flock` on the sidecar itself cannot work: the lock is on the inode, so a writer blocked on it wakes after the swap and appends into an unlinked file.

  Three `raise e` become bare `raise` (`persistence.py`), so the traceback is not truncated at the re-raising frame. Two more of the same shape were found and deliberately left, being outside this issue: `sidecar.py`'s decompress handler — whose entire `try`/`except` does nothing but re-raise — and one in `entities.py`.


- **Every test that opened a `Session` and walked away now closes it, and a contract test makes the class unwritable (#371).** 36 modules across 58 construction sites. No package code changes.

  **The symptom was cosmetic and the defect was not.** Twice on `test (3.12)` — run 34060523498 on `e193ea7`, a docs commit, and run 34125623192 on an unrelated PR branch — the whole job went red as `1542 passed, 1 error`, the error being `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'tests_data_naming'` from `shutil.rmtree` in `teardown_module`. Every test had passed; only the cleanup failed, and it failed on a file nothing in either commit touched. That is the worst shape a red can have: it costs whoever is holding a PR the time to prove the failure is not theirs, which is exactly what it cost here before this was filed.

  **What was actually wrong.** `test_folder_naming_structure` built its session with a bare `DicomSession(db_path)` and never closed it. Measured on this tree, with a probe that counts before and after a single ingest-and-export:

  | | Threads leaked | Child processes leaked |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | bare constructor | **5** | **5** |
  | `with` block | 0 | 0 |

  The five threads are `AuditWorker`, `PersistenceWorker`, `QueueFeederThread`, `Thread-1` and `tqdm_monitor`. The first two hold sqlite handles on `tests_data_naming/isocenter.db`, which lives *inside* the directory the teardown then removes — and SQLite creates and drops `-wal`/`-shm` files without asking, so `os.path.exists(TEST_DIR)` said yes and `rmtree` raised on a path that had gone by the time it walked there. The log immediately above the error shows `Saving 1 patients to tests_data_naming/isocenter.db (Incremental)` twice, after the test body had returned, which is the background save still running during the teardown.

  **The leak is the reason to fix it, not the noise.** `close()` releases a `ProcessPoolExecutor` plus those two sqlite threads; skipping it leaves them for the remainder of the pytest process. A suite that has been bitten by load-dependent races as often as this one (#250, #343, #274, #297) cannot afford tests that leave five subprocesses running behind them — every later test in the run becomes slightly less deterministic, and the failures that produces land somewhere else entirely. `shutil.rmtree(..., ignore_errors=True)` was rejected for exactly that reason: it would have made the red go away and left the leak.

  Green five times in a row after the change, where the flake was intermittent before.

  **The whole population is fixed, and it was larger than the grep that found it said.** The sweep that turned this one up -- top-level `tests/*.py` containing `DicomSession(` and containing neither `with DicomSession` nor `.close()` -- reported 29 modules. It is a file-level test of a per-site property, so it is wrong in both directions, and `tests/test_packaging_contract.py::test_a_session_a_test_opens_is_a_session_the_test_closes` (new, below) reports **36 modules across 58 construction sites** on the same tree. The seven it missed are three separate ways a file-level grep is wrong, and all three are worth writing down. `tests/test_unified_config.py` spells the constructor `Session`, the alias the grep did not look for. `test_analysis`, `test_analysis_persistence` and `test_optimization` contain `conn.close()` -- a sqlite connection, not a session. `test_api_coherence` and `test_wfdb_conformance` contain a real `session.close()` belonging to a *different* session several tests away from the leaking one. And `test_sidecar` was excluded on **prose**: its docstring reads "Test full integration with DicomSession", which the `with DicomSession` exclusion counted as a context manager.

  **What each site leaked varies, and 5/5 is the ceiling rather than the rule.** The five-and-five above is `test_folder_naming_structure`, which ingests and exports. Two more sites measured the same way, before and after: `test_scaffold_features.py::test_scaffold_config_structure` (`:memory:`, config scaffolding only) leaked **2 threads and 0 child processes**, now 0 and 0; `test_reversibility.py::test_reversible_anonymization_flow` (file-backed, anonymize and export) leaked **3 threads and 0 child processes**, now 1 -- and that one is `tqdm_monitor`, a daemon thread tqdm owns and `Session.close()` has no claim on. The pool's workers are spawned on demand, so a session that never dispatches parallel work leaks the executor without leaking processes. Every one of them leaks `AuditWorker` and `PersistenceWorker`, and those are the two that hold sqlite handles.

  **Two of the sites were a teardown that read as cleanup and was not.** `tests/test_metadata_refactor_full.py` and `tests/test_redaction_parallel.py` both had a `tearDown` calling `self.session.store_backend.stop()`. That releases the audit-log writer and nothing else: the `ProcessPoolExecutor` and the persistence thread stayed. Both now call `close()`. `tests/test_reporting_features.py`'s `populated_session` fixture `return`ed its session, which no test requesting a fixture has an idiom for closing; it `yield`s and closes now.

  **`with` is the shape used wherever it fits, and it did not fit everywhere.** `tests/test_session.py::test_session_persistence` and `tests/test_sidecar.py::test_session_sidecar_persistence` each open a second session on the same database to read back what the first wrote; both are **nested**, not sequenced, because the first session was still open when the second read and closing it early would silently change the question to "reopen after close" -- a different test that neither module says it is running. The two `unittest.TestCase` classes keep `tearDown`, which runs before the `tmpdir` removal that `addCleanup` would follow.

  **What the guard pins, and what it does not.** It parses each top-level test module and requires every construction of a name imported from `isocenter`/`isocenter.session` as `Session` or `DicomSession` -- resolved from the imports, so an `as` rename is still seen -- to be a `with`, an assignment whose name is closed later in the same function, a `self.x = ...` closed anywhere in its class, a `return`ed factory result (except from a `@pytest.fixture`, which has no caller that would close it), or a registration into a list a fixture teardown drains. It checks **spelling, not reachability**: a `close()` in a branch that does not run satisfies it, which is why `with` is the preferred shape and the test says so in its own docstring rather than in this entry alone. It carries a vacuity floor on recognised construction sites, for the reason its sibling `test_every_top_level_tests_module_is_one_pytest_collects` carries one: a sweep that finds nothing finds no offenders either.


- **#250 is closed: the intermittent 3.12/ubuntu hang was the `fork` start method, and #260 fixed it in 0.9.1. The release runbook now dispatches the probe before each tag (#250).** No package code changes here. `.agent/workflows/release_process.md` gains step 1a; the evidence is below, because an issue closed on a measurement should carry the measurement.

  **What was run.** `.github/workflows/hang-probe.yml`, twice, both on `e484bee` so the iterations combine: run `34073209412` (`start_method=both`) and run `34113535260` (`spawn` only). Each iteration is the whole suite on ubuntu / 3.12 -- the platform and interpreter #250 was opened on.

  | Arm | Iterations | Result |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `fork` | 1 | **HANG at 945s**, killed by the probe's own deadline |
  | `spawn` | 10 + 10 | **20/20 clean**, 576-756s each |

  That is the pre-registered decision table's first row -- "spawn >= 20 clean and fork `HANG`/`LOCKED` within 10: #250 closes as fixed by #260" -- and it is the row the run landed on.

  **The `fork` hang is not a live defect, and reading it as one is the mistake this entry exists to prevent.** All four pool sites pin `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` and have since #260: `parallel.py` at the `ProcessPoolExecutor` and the recycling `Pool`, and `session.py` at `_executor` and its OOM restart. The probe's `fork` arm re-creates the removed population deliberately, by rebinding `multiprocessing.get_context` in `tests/conftest.py`. So the arm reproduces the *pre-#260* library, and what it establishes is that the fork hypothesis behind #250 was correct and that #260 answered it -- not that anything shipped today deadlocks.

  **What the dump shows, and what it does not.** The parent stack is `audit()` -> `run_parallel` -> `_run_on_new_executor` -> `result()`, blocked, with `AuditWorker` and `PersistenceWorker` threads resident and four `ForkProcess` children alive. It hung in `tests/test_analysis.py::test_phi_report_analysis`, **not** the test #250 names, which is what makes it start-method-specific rather than test-specific. The dump is **parent-only** -- the four children were never dumped -- so *which* lock they inherited held is inferred, not measured. Stated as inference on purpose: the tree has been bitten before by a plausible mechanism written down as a fact.

  **Which historical occurrences it matches.** Zero `database is locked` and zero `OperationalError` in the hanging iteration's log, so this reproduces occurrences 1-3 (the silent ~900s stall) and not 4-5 (the sqlite error from a forked child). Whether those two share this mechanism is not established here.

  **The cadence, because a probe nobody dispatches is a probe that does not exist.** Before each release, `spawn` arm, ten iterations, run by whoever cuts the release and read before tagging; ten clean is the pass and a `HANG` reopens #250. Not scheduled: a multi-hour job on a timer is a CI cost decision, and not on the PR gate for the same reason.

  **It is written in two places on purpose.** The operational step is `.agent/workflows/release_process.md` step 1a -- but that directory is **gitignored**, so it exists only on the release-cutter's machine. A commitment recorded only in an untracked file is one the next contributor cannot read, and this entry would otherwise be asserting a process nothing in the repository carries. So the cadence, the pass condition and the reason the arm is `spawn` rather than `both` are also in `.github/workflows/hang-probe.yml`'s header, which ships. (`both` doubles the runtime to re-prove a settled negative and turns the run red on the arm that is *supposed* to fail.)

- **A zero-length private element is written as the element it is, not dropped as a loss (#344).** One branch in `DicomExporter._merge`'s private arm and one documentation-only guard at the top of `_value_fits_vr`, both in `isocenter/io_handlers.py`; the assertions in `tests/test_private_tag_empty_value_roundtrip.py` reverse. **This is a grade change, and it goes up.** On the reference fixture, ingest -> audit -> scan_pixel_content -> export -> report measured `REVIEW_REQUIRED` with **12 `DATA_LOSS` rows** before and **`PASS` with 0** after, and the warning that stops appearing is:

      WARNING: <uid>: Tag 0009,1005 not exported (data loss): no VR fits a NoneType value

  **A grade going up is the one that needs the argument, so here it is.** Before: twelve elements in the source, zero in the copy, twelve rows saying so -- the rows were *correct* and `REVIEW_REQUIRED` was the honest grade for a copy missing twelve elements. After: twelve in the source, twelve in the copy, nothing to report. The `PASS` is earned by the export getting better, not by the report getting quieter, and the population that stops filing rows is exactly the population that stops losing elements. `test_neither_export_reports_a_loss_for_the_empty_block` asserts both halves in one place so the two can never come apart. A run with any other loss keeps its `REVIEW_REQUIRED`: the grade is a conjunction over all graded rows, and nothing here sweeps anything to PASS.

  **What is written.** A present, zero-length element under the tag's **recorded VR** where `attribute_vrs` has one, and under **`UN`** where it does not. `UN` is what PS3.5 6.2.2 says an element of unknown VR is, and it is the arm *every* private element of an Implicit VR Little Endian source takes, because `_record_private_vr` refuses to record `UN` by design.

  **The population is eleven recorded VRs plus the no-VR case, not the eight #339's test and #344's text name.** Measured by writing a zero-length private element under every VR pydicom accepts and asking `_record_private_vr` what it would record: `DS`, `IS`, `US`, `SS`, `UL`, `SL`, `UV`, `SV`, `FL`, `FD`, `AT` all read back `None` and all record their source VR; `UN` reads back `None` and records nothing; `OB`/`OW`/`OD`/`OF`/`OL` never reach the recorder because `BINARY_VRS` converts them to `b""` first; the text VRs read back `''` and already exported correctly. **`SL`, `SV` and `UV` were missing from both lists** -- they are not in `BINARY_VRS`, are not `SQ`, `PN` or `UN`, so they take `populate_attrs`' final `else` arm with `elem.value is None` and are recorded like the other eight. They are three new rows in the test's parametrisation and behave identically.

  **Why not the one-line fallback-`LO` answer.** `_fallback_multivalue` already writes `('LO', [])` for the empty-list case, and reusing that shape here needs no change to `_value_fits_vr` at all. It writes a `DS` tag out as `LO` -- a different infidelity, not a smaller one, and the exact throwing-away of the source's own answer that #154 exists to stop.

  **Why `_value_fits_vr` was not widened, measured.** The obvious mechanism is a global `if value is None: return True`, and it is the one dangerous option. That function recurses over a list, so it would make `_value_fits_vr([None, 'B'], 'LO')` return `True`; `add_new(Tag(0x0009,0x1030), 'LO', [None, 'B'])` then **succeeds**, and the failure lands in `filewriter`:

      TypeError: With tag (0009,1030) got exception:
          sequence item 0: expected a bytes-like object, NoneType found

  That raises *past* `_merge`'s `try` and **fails the whole file rather than the element** -- precisely the second failure class `_value_fits_vr`'s own docstring was written to prevent, arriving through `write_text` instead of `write_numbers`. The branch is therefore in `_merge`, one level above, where the two populations cannot overlap: a scalar `None` is intercepted before `_value_fits_vr` is asked anything, and a `None` *inside* a list never meets the interception because `[None, 'B'] is not None`. `test_a_none_among_siblings_is_the_same_loud_loss_on_both_paths` is the test that catches the widen, and its docstring now says so. `_value_fits_vr`, `_fallback_encoding` and `_fallback_multivalue` are otherwise untouched.

  The explicit `if value is None: return False` added at the top of `_value_fits_vr` is documentation and changes nothing -- `None` already reached the closing `return False` by matching no `isinstance` arm. **It is an equivalent mutant on purpose**: deleting it, or flipping its `False` to `True`, leaves every test green, because `_merge`'s branch runs first and nothing else reaches the function with a `None`. `scripts/mutation_probe` will report it as survived; that is not a test gap and must not be closed by writing a test around it. It is there because it is where a future reader who tries to "clean up" the `_merge` branch will look.

  **One sentence of #339's entry is superseded.** That entry says: *"`_split_core_and_private` is left exactly as it was. #60's ruling is honoured: the file still omits the tag, on both paths."* The first sentence stays true -- this change has no persistence half, and the reloaded `attributes` and `attribute_vrs` were measured identical to the fresh ones, `None` values and recorded VRs included. The second becomes false: the file now carries the tag on both paths. The reading it rested on was wrong. **#60's ruling itself is untouched**, and this is an instance of it rather than an exception. #60 forbids *inventing* a value where the source supplied none, and the sentinel `19000101` claimed a fact the file never stated; a zero-length `DS` claims no fact at all -- it asserts exactly what the source asserted, that the tag is present and has no value, in the one encoding DICOM provides for saying it. #60's own second clause has been pointing this way the whole time: *"not one we invent **and not one we discard**"*. Dropping the element is the discard half, and this repo had been doing it to this population since #118. #60 predates `docs/superpowers/specs/` and its ruling lives only in this changelog -- checked with a grep of that directory, not assumed -- so nothing there carries a `Superseded in part:` marker; the mechanism is that a new entry names what it supersedes, which is this paragraph.

  **A hand-written `set_attr(tag, None)` on a recorded-`LO` private tag now writes `LO ''` where it used to be dropped**, and this reverses a test whose *name* asserted the old direction: `test_a_none_written_by_hand_onto_a_text_vr_private_tag_is_not_invented` becomes `..._takes_that_vr`. The rule is followed uniformly, deliberately. The `None` there came from a caller rather than from a file -- and from nowhere inside `isocenter/`, which was checked rather than asserted: the removal arms *delete* the key (`del entity.attributes[proposal.target_attr]`, `inst.attributes.pop(tag, None)`) and none of them writes a `None` value, so the shape is reachable only from user code. It is still not fabrication: the recorded VR is a fact about the *source element*, which was present, `set_attr` does not clear `attribute_vrs`, and a zero-length element invents nothing. Telling a file-borne `None` from a hand-set one would need a provenance flag the graph does not carry, and following the rule uniformly is what keeps this one branch rather than two.

  **Both export paths gain it in one edit and cannot gain it separately.** `session.export()` and `DicomExporter.write_tree()` both reach `_export_instance_worker`, which calls `_merge` with the instance's `attribute_vrs`; `_merge_sequences`' item merge passes `vrs` the same way, so a nested private element gains the behaviour at the same time. `tests/test_api_coherence.py` did **not** go red for this and is not the evidence -- it guards against a future fork of the two paths, not this change. The **no-`DATA_LOSS`-row** half is identical on both paths for a different reason: `write_tree` has no store handle and logs a warning where `session.export()` files a row. Both stop happening, from the same cause.

  **Under the export's default transfer syntax the VR half of the decision is invisible**, and this is recorded so it is not rediscovered as a bug. `_create_ds` sets Implicit VR Little Endian, which carries no VR on the wire and for which a reader has no dictionary entry for a private tag -- so every private element reads back as `UN` whatever was written, at an identical **474 bytes for all nineteen VRs measured**. Only the compressed branch replaces the syntax with an explicit-VR one. The element's *presence* is the half that matters on both branches; the recorded-VR-vs-`UN` choice is observable only on the explicit branch, which is why the fixture in `tests/test_private_tag_empty_value_roundtrip.py` carries pixel data and says so in a docstring, and why the new assertions read the VR off the file rather than the tag's presence alone.

  **Not folded in, and not touched: `_fallback_multivalue([]) -> ('LO', [])`.** An *empty list* under a recorded `DS` is still written as `LO`, because `_value_fits_vr([], 'DS')` is `False` through its `bool(value)` clause and the recorded VR is never consulted. That is the same infidelity one shape over, but it is a different population -- pydicom never yields `[]` for a zero-length element, it yields `None`, so `[]` is reachable only from a hand `set_attr` -- and this change's whole value is that its population is measured. It is tracked separately as #367, and `tests/test_private_tag_export.py:386` is left exactly as it stands.

- **The hang probe could not be dispatched at all: its two computed `timeout-minutes` made the workflow unparseable (#250).** `.github/workflows/hang-probe.yml`'s job cap and loop-step cap are now the literals `356` and `340`; `tests/test_packaging_contract.py::test_the_hang_probe_never_runs_on_the_gate` gains the assertion that would have caught it.

  **What happened.** The probe merged with its caps written as a product of the dispatch inputs plus a constant -- `iterations * per_iteration_minutes + 25` for the job, `+ 5` for the loop step -- and the first dispatch attempt answered:

      HTTP 422: failed to parse workflow: (Line: 102, Col: 22): Unexpected symbol: '+'.
      Located at position 70 within expression: fromJSON(inputs.iterations) *
      fromJSON(inputs.per_iteration_minutes) + 25 ... (Line: 166, Col: 24): same for + 5

  **Why.** **GitHub Actions expressions have no arithmetic operators.** The documented set is `( ) [ ] . ! < <= > >= == != && ||` -- no `+`, `-`, `*` or `/` -- so a cap cannot be derived from the inputs by any spelling, and a file containing one fails to *parse*: not the step, not the job, the whole workflow. It sat on `main` inert, and nothing said so, because the only thing that runs it is a manual dispatch.

  **What replaced it.** Two literals sized for the documented input ceiling (22 iterations x 15 minutes = 330) rather than for the inputs of any one run: loop step 340, job 356. The required inequality is unchanged and now reads directly -- 356 > 340 + 15 (the five literal 3s), and 356 is inside GitHub's 360-minute job maximum -- so whatever hangs, the timeout that fires still belongs to a step (#243). The trade is stated at both sites: the caps no longer track a short run, which makes them a pure backstop, and that is what they already were in practice, since the loop script declares `HANG` at `per_iteration_minutes` and a step cap firing means the script itself is stuck. The `iterations` input's own description carries the new ceiling arithmetic.

  **The guard was grading the arithmetic's text, not its validity -- and that is the lesson worth more than the fix.** `test_the_hang_probe_never_runs_on_the_gate` parsed the `+ N` tail out of each cap string and compared the two constants, so it asserted the inequality correctly and **passed on a workflow GitHub refuses to load**. A test that is green on a file nothing can parse is worse than no test: it converts "nobody checked" into "something checked". The replacement asserts on the raw `${{ }}` bodies that no expression in the file contains an arithmetic character, quotes the 422 in its failure message, and reads the two caps as plain integers; string literals are stripped before the scan so a hyphen inside one is not read as subtraction, and the scan is deliberately *inside* the expressions only, because the loop script's `deadline=$(( ${{ inputs.per_iteration_minutes }} * 60 ))` is bash arithmetic and legitimate. Verified by reintroducing the merged spelling: the new assertion fails naming `['*', '+']`.

  Nothing else about the probe changed -- same triggers, same loop script, same two conftest hooks -- so the `Added` entry above still describes what it does. **Final proof is a dispatch**, which needs this on the default branch first.

- **`get_flattened_instances([])` walked the whole store (#142).** `SqliteStore._iter_flattened_instances` gated its two filters with truth tests -- `if patient_ids:` and `if instance_uids:` -- so an empty list read as "no filter" and returned every row in the store. Both gates are now `is not None`.

  **What a previously-working call now does.** `store.get_flattened_instances(patient_ids=[])` and `store.get_flattened_instances(instance_uids=[])` return no rows, where they returned every row. `None` still means every patient. Nothing else changes: a non-empty list filters exactly as before, and both filters together intersect (a test now pins that too -- each alone was covered, the conjunction was not).

  **Why the old behaviour was wrong.** The in-memory readers already said the opposite, in code and in a test: `get_cohort_report` uses `patient_ids is not None and p.patient_id not in patient_ids` with the comment "`[]` must exclude everyone. A caller computing a cohort that came back empty would otherwise export the whole dataset"; `_export_dicom` is the same `is not None`; `tests/test_dataframe_export.py::test_an_empty_patient_id_list_selects_nobody` states the rule. Three readers, two spellings of "empty", and the one that got it wrong was the DB reader the 0.9.1 CHANGELOG names as the migration path for callers of the deleted `export_to_parquet` -- so a caller who followed that advice, computed a cohort, and got an empty one back would have streamed the entire index. That is a silent over-export in exactly the shape the sibling's comment warns about.

  **Why there is no short-circuit.** The empty list renders `p.patient_id IN ()`, which SQLite accepts as legal and false -- a dialect extension, not SQL. From sqlite.org/lang_expr.html: "SQLite allows the parenthesized list of scalar values on the right-hand side of an IN or NOT IN operator to be an empty list but most other SQL database engines and the SQL92 standard require the list to contain at least one element." An explicit `return` for `[]` would be a second mechanism for one rule; the comment at the gate quotes the sentence so a port to another engine knows it needs one. The two empty-list tests drain through `list(...)` on a `:memory:` store and are the proof the gate's SQLite accepts the construct, on both interpreters the PR gate runs.

  **#142 itself is closed as keep.** The method is public API -- `docs/api/persistence.md` renders `isocenter.persistence` unfiltered, and the 0.9.1 CHANGELOG names it -- with no in-tree caller by decision (#55 chose the in-memory graph for `export_dataframe`). Its coverage is anchored on the method itself, which has been lost twice to deletions elsewhere (`generate_export_from_db`, then `export_to_parquet`); the holding-action test is promoted to `test_get_flattened_instances_is_public_api_covered_on_itself` with its three assertions intact, and its signature -- `(self, patient_ids, instance_uids, page_size)` -- is pinned in `tests/test_api_coherence.py` as the surface #26 will freeze. The `:memory:` deadlock the issue's comment describes was fixed in 0.9.1 (#164), which also gave `instance_uids` its coverage; there was nothing left to design there, and the walk is untouched.

- **`session.export()` completes its save before it frees memory, so which instances reach the export workers no longer depends on a thread race (#343).** One line in `Session._export_dicom`: `self.save()` is `self.save(sync=True)`. New `tests/test_export_flushes_before_it_sweeps.py`.

  **What it did.** `_export_dicom` called `save()` -- `persistence_manager.save_async()`, which enqueues and returns -- and then `release_memory()`, under a comment saying "flush before the walk". It did not flush before the walk; it flushed *concurrently with* it. `release_memory()` frees an instance only once the background save has attached its `_pixel_loader`, so which instances were swept depended on which thread got there first. On an idle machine the sweep won, every unload was refused, and the resident arrays reached the export workers. Under CPU contention the save won for some subset of the graph and those instances were nulled and reloaded through the loader -- a different subset on every run. For an ingested instance the reload is correct and the race was benign: nondeterministic memory behaviour, same output, which is how it survived. For an instance whose `pixel_array` had been assigned directly, with no Rows/Columns ever written, the reload came back as an empty image and the export failed with `Compression failed: cannot write empty image` and an `ExportError` -- `tests/test_wfdb_writer.py`'s colocation test, and the issue's exact text. Measured: **0/200** sweeps on an idle machine, **2/300** with two full suites running beside it (load 11-34 on 14 cores), that test failing **4 runs in 15** under the same load, and deterministic in both directions with the order forced.

  **The tree had met this race once and fixed the other half.** The 0.9.2 entry for #183 (float16) records it: "`session.export()`'s `save()` is asynchronous, so the unload in `release_memory()` was usually refused -- no loader had been bound yet ... Once the save won that race, the reload returned `uint16`". That fixed the dtype the reload came back with and left the ordering as it was.

  **The trade.** `save(sync=True)` drains the manager and then runs `save_all` on the exporting thread, and it inherits `flush()`'s never-return-early property -- a genuinely wedged worker now wedges the export instead of racing it -- which is the trade `save()`'s own docstring argues for. `audit()` and `redact()` already drained on entry (#297, #274); export was the third verb and did not. The new test slows `save_all` by half a second on whichever thread calls it and records, in order, the thread the save returned on, the sweep starting, and the state the sweep left (`loader attached, array nulled, queue empty`): red before the change as `(False, False, 1)` with the save returning later on `PersistenceWorker`; green after as the export's own save on the exporting thread, followed by a reload that wrote a real image. A "wedged save is visible" test is deliberately not written -- a test that waits forever is not a test.

  **Closing the sessions -- the issue's offered fact -- was measured and does not change the rate.** The race loop closes every session and still hits 2/300; the race is inside one `export()` call and a session's lifetime has no bearing on it. Both `DicomSession(":memory:")` sites in `tests/test_wfdb_writer.py` become `with` blocks anyway, because an unclosed session leaks an executor and two threads, and the colocation fixture's `instance.pixel_array = ...` becomes `instance.set_pixel_data(...)` so the instance carries the Rows/Columns it needs to survive its own export -- with the synchronous save, the direct assignment fails deterministically (1 failed / 22 passed before the fixture edit) rather than one run in four under load. `tests/test_close_warns_about_unsaved_instances.py`'s exported-session measurement said the save was asynchronous; its docstring now says why it is kept when it is not.

- **`SidecarPixelLoader` refuses a frame whose declared geometry is zero instead of returning an empty image with the integrity hash passing (#343).** One guard in `SidecarPixelLoader.__call__`; two tests in `tests/test_pixel_geometry_pipeline.py`.

  When the reshape to the declared geometry fails, the loader falls back to a truncate-then-reshape meant for the one-byte DICOM pad: `target_size = rows * cols * ...; if arr.size >= target_size: arr = arr[:target_size]`. With no Rows/Columns on the instance the declared geometry is `(0, 0)`, `target_size` is 0, `arr.size >= 0` is always true, `arr[:0]` is empty, and a `(0, 0)` uint8 array went back to the caller -- with the integrity hash passing, because the hash is over the raw bytes and runs before the reshape. The export worker then failed on the empty image; a caller who never exports got `get_pixel_data()` returning something that looked like data. It now raises `RuntimeError("Integrity Error: <uid> declares no pixel geometry (Rows=0, Columns=0, Frames=0); a stored frame of N bytes cannot be reshaped to nothing")` -- the same family and prefix as the hash mismatch six lines above it, so it rides the export worker's existing `Pixel Loader failed for ...` handling into an `ERROR` audit row and a `REVIEW_REQUIRED` grade, and a caller's `get_pixel_data()` raises rather than answers. Returning `None` was rejected: `get_pixel_data()` would fall through to `file_path` and return `None`, and the worker's `arr is None` arm would export a non-image modality with no pixels, silently. The guard is in `__call__`'s body and not a wrapper, because the loader pickles into spawned export workers and a guard installed on the parent would not be in the child.

  **Exactly `target_size == 0` and nothing wider.** `arr.size != target_size` would break every odd-length source, whose one-byte pad is what the fallback exists for -- `test_a_frame_with_one_byte_of_dicom_padding_still_reshapes` pins a 5-byte 2x2 frame reshaping to `(2, 2)` with the pad dropped. `target_size` is the quantity the fallback compares `arr.size` against, so it names exactly the case the fallback mishandles; `frames` enters the shape only when greater than 1 and `samples` is normalised to at least 1, so it is zero exactly when Rows or Columns is (Rows=2, Columns=2, Frames=0 loads as `(2, 2)`). The guard runs *ahead of the reshape*, not inside its `except`: an empty frame reshapes to `(0, 0)` without raising, so a guard in the fallback never saw it -- a second test pins the 0-byte case. **Filed rather than fixed**: the fallback still tolerates *any* surplus (`arr[:target_size]` drops every byte past the declared geometry, not just the one pad byte) and still returns a flat 1-D array on any shortfall (`return arr  # Fallback to 1D`), both of which hand descriptor damage to a caller as a healthy array; and a resident `waveform_array` with no loader is never written by `save_all` and never exported to DICOM, which is the `Waveform Sequence present but no samples are available to export` DATA_LOSS row the colocation test files on every run, green or red, and is not part of this failure.
- **`ISOCENTER_CHUNKSIZE=0` now warns naming the variable and the value and falls back to `1`; before it fell back in silence (#341).** `ISOCENTER_CHUNKSIZE=-1` now warns and falls back to `1`; before it was carried into the pool: silently ignored on the threads path (`ThreadPoolExecutor.map` discards `chunksize`), `ValueError: chunksize must be >= 1.` from `ProcessPoolExecutor.map`, and `ValueError: Chunksize must be 1+, not -1` from `multiprocessing.Pool.imap` on the recycling path, none of them naming the variable. **A call that raised now succeeds.** The read was `_env_int("ISOCENTER_CHUNKSIZE") or 1` -- the exact `or` the 0.9.2 #335 entry removed one line above it, for the exact reason that entry gives: `0` is the one value that must be reported and the one value that is falsey, and a negative is truthy and travels.

  **`ISOCENTER_MAX_WORKERS` below 1 on the redaction path now warns and uses that path's default; before it was clamped to a single worker in silence.** `_redaction_worker_count` (`isocenter/session.py`, whose only caller is `redact()`) reads the variable itself and passes the answer to `run_parallel` as an explicit `max_workers`, so the read #335 guarded never sees the environment there. It settled the override with `max(1, override)`: `0` became one worker and so did `-1`, with nothing said. Measured on a 14-CPU box: `0` -> `1` silently, `-1` -> `1` silently, `banana` -> `7` with a warning, `3` -> `3`. **This corrects a sentence in the 0.9.2 #335 entry and in `docs/environment.md`'s `ISOCENTER_MAX_WORKERS` row**: both said a value below 1 "is reported with a warning naming the variable and the value, and the default is used instead", and that was true of `run_parallel` and false of `redact()`, because the variable is read in two files and #335 guarded one. The 0.9.2 entry is left standing and corrected here rather than rewritten; the docs row now says the redaction path reads the variable too, and rejects the same way. The redaction default itself -- half the CPUs, capped at eight, a memory ceiling -- is unchanged and is a separate question from the one this entry settles.

  **The floor moves into the helper: `_env_int(name, *, minimum)`, keyword-only, no default.** All four reads in the package pass `minimum=1` -- three in `_resolve_strategy`, one in `_redaction_worker_count`. Below the floor the helper warns naming the variable, the value and the floor, and returns `None`, so each call site's existing "`None` means the documented default" fallback supplies the default exactly as it already does for `banana`. The 0.9.2 #335 entry declined this shape because "exactly one call site would ever pass it", and the 0.9.2 #185 entry deferred it to "#341 is where that is decided"; the count is now four reads of three variables, one of them read in two places, and that is the fact that decided it -- a floor at a call site is a floor at one of the places a variable is read. Two shapes rejected: a default of `1` makes the floor invisible at the read site and turns a future integer variable that legitimately accepts `0` into a silent rejection; a default of `None` lets a fifth read site inherit #335's defect by omission. Requiring the keyword means every read states its floor or states `minimum=None`, and either way a reader sees it. The two hand-written `< 1` arms in `_resolve_strategy`, and their comments explaining why the floor was *not* in `_env_int`, are deleted; the `or`-trap explanation moves onto `_env_int`'s docstring, which is the one place every reader of the helper passes.

  **Shipped log text changes for two variables.** `ISOCENTER_MAX_WORKERS is set to 0, which is not a usable worker count. Ignoring it and using the default. Set it to 1 to run with a single worker.` and `ISOCENTER_MAX_TASKS_PER_CHILD is set to 0, which is not a usable number of tasks per worker. Ignoring it and recycling no workers. Set it to 1 or more to recycle.` both become `<VARIABLE> is set to <value>, which is below the minimum of 1. Ignoring it and using the default.` -- one spelling, variable, value and floor named. The per-variable advice those two tails carried lives only in the `docs/environment.md` rows now, which already had it; two hand-written tails for one behaviour were two spellings of it. The existing #335 and #185 tests assert the variable name and `set to 0` / `-1` / `-5` substrings and stay green against the new text.

  No value that worked changes meaning: unset, `1`, `2`, `5` and `banana` behave exactly as before for all three variables, and an explicit `max_workers=0` / `maxtasksperchild=0` *argument* still reaches the pool and still raises there (the two #335/#185 tests pinning arm placement are untouched). New: an 18-cell matrix in `tests/test_parallel_contract.py` holding all three variables to one answer at once (`{unset, 1, 2, 0, -3, banana}` per variable; **red on exactly two cells when written, `CHUNKSIZE-0` and `CHUNKSIZE--3`**, with the `1` cells there to tell `<` from `<=`), two direct `_env_int` tests (red on `TypeError`, floor of 5 so a return-the-floor mutant cannot hide behind a one-CPU runner's defaults), and `tests/test_redaction_worker_count.py` (red on the value *and* the silence on a multi-CPU box -- `1` against a default of `7` here; on a one- or two-CPU runner the default is also `1` and only the silence is red, which its docstring says so a small-runner log is not misread).

- **A source citation written across a line break is now graded by both rules of `tests/test_source_citations.py`; before, one wrapped between `at` and the path was range-checked but never content-checked, one wrapped between the path and `line` was checked by neither rule, and one wrapped inside a `#` comment was invisible to both even after joining the text (#346).** One helper (`_citations`), one regex fragment (`_GAP`), both scanners and the module docstring in that file; three new fixture tests. A repair to a test guard, the same class as the #310, #324 and #325 entries.

  Both grammars join their tokens with `\s+`, which crosses a newline, and both scanners handed them one line at a time, so a wrapped citation matched the regex and was never given the chance to. Measured with a fixture module and the wrong citation `` `second()` at zzz_fixture_mod.py line 2 `` (`second()` is line 3) at four wrap positions: between `at` and the path -- Rule 2 not checked, Rule 1 graded (so it *looked* pinned, which is the dangerous half); between the path and `line` -- checked by neither; between `line` and the number -- checked by neither; between the code span and `at` -- Rule 2 not checked, Rule 1 graded. Over the joined text both regexes match all four. On the live tree: 48 Rule 1 and 15 Rule 2 raw matches per line, 48 and 15 over the joined text -- **zero wrapped citations exist today**, so this was latent, exactly as the issue says.

  **A fifth case the issue does not name.** Six of the 48 Rule 1 matches sit on `#` comment lines. A citation wrapped inside a comment reads `` `code` at\n# path.py line N `` once joined -- a newline, a `#`, a space -- and `\s+` does not cross the `#`. Measured: with the scanners on joined text and the regexes unchanged, the after-`at` and before-`line` fixtures go green and the comment-continuation fixture stays red. So the gap between tokens becomes `\s+(?:#[ \t]*)?` in both grammars. The code span itself stays `[^`\n]+`: a code span cannot wrap.

  **What the scan is now.** Each scanner matches the file's whole text and derives the line from the match offset (`text.count("\n", 0, match.start()) + 1`), reporting the line the citation *starts* on. This mirrors `tests/test_documented_env_vars.py`'s `_names_read`, which already does exactly this for environment reads and gives the same reason. The target side is untouched: `lines[number - 1]` and Rule 1's length still come from `splitlines()`, and `test_the_check_would_fail_on_an_off_by_one_citation`, which asserts `notes.md:2:` for a single-line citation on line 2, is the regression guard for the offset arithmetic. The three new fixtures put an `Intro.` line first so the wrapped citation starts on line 2 and ends on 3, which is what tells a `match.start()` derivation from `match.end()` and from a dropped `+ 1`.

  **Measured after the change:** Rule 1 graded 23 and Rule 2 checked 11, both unchanged; the set of matches produced by the widened regexes over every graded file is identical to the old regexes' set -- zero matches new to the widening; zero matches spanning a newline anywhere in the tree. The raw Rule 1 count reads 51 rather than 48 only because the three new tests carry three `zzz_fixture_mod.py line 2` literals of their own, which resolve to no file and are graded by nothing (the eight existing fixture tests contribute to the 48 the same way). The vacuity floors stay at 10 and 5 rather than being raised to the measured 23 and 11: a floor pinned to today's count is a test of today's count.

  **One known widening**, stated in the module docstring: over joined text a bare path ending one line followed by `line N` starting the next now reads as a citation even across a sentence boundary. Zero in the tree; if it ever fires on prose that is right, the fix is to reword the prose, because a sentence shaped like a citation deserves to be one. **Rejected:** the issue's second option, a per-line scan that goes red on a partial match ending in `at` -- it needs one partial pattern per wrap position plus comment variants, teaches the writer instead of grading the citation, and the issue's own widening comment already preferred the joined scan for closing every case with one pattern. **Rejected:** joined text without the comment gap -- closes four cases and knowingly leaves the fifth, in a guard whose whole subject is unmarked opt-outs.

  Housekeeping worth recording: #346 was auto-closed once by the word `fixed` preceding its number inside a sentence saying it was *not* fixed, and reopened. This entry's cross-references are written so that no closing keyword precedes an issue number it is not closing.

- **Prose that cited `tests/profile_memory.py` as one of the files defending the export subprocess boundary now says the file was deleted and that eight files, not nine, rest on it (#347).** `_run_export_batch`'s docstring in `isocenter/session.py` and `test_export_runs_in_processes_by_decision`'s docstring and inline comment in `tests/test_parallel_contract.py`. **This corrects the 0.9.2 #185 entry**, which counts "the nine test files that rest on processes-on-export" and "names the eight test files plus `tests/profile_memory.py`"; the count is eight, the 0.9.2 entry is left standing, and the ninth is named in the new prose only as history -- as the uncollected file that had drifted to `10`, deleted here -- so nobody goes looking for it. The `maxtasksperchild=25` contract the file claimed to check **was already pinned four times by collected tests**, so nothing moved because there was nothing to move: `tests/test_parallel_contract.py::test_export_runs_in_processes_by_decision` (captures the kwargs `_run_export_batch` passes, asserts `25`, and ties `_use_threads`'s log sentence to that captured number), `tests/test_shared_executor_lifecycle.py` (asserts `kwargs['maxtasksperchild'] == 25`), `tests/test_parallel_contract.py::test_a_raising_task_is_yielded_as_a_value_on_the_recycling_pool` (the Pool path selected by `maxtasksperchild`), and `tests/test_parallel_config.py::test_run_parallel_maxtasksperchild` (the Pool constructed with the value).

### Removed

- **`tests/profile_memory.py`, `tests/detect_memory_leak.py` and `tests/profile_export_memory.py` are deleted (#347).** No dependency is added, nothing is relocated, and a new contract test in `tests/test_packaging_contract.py` -- `test_every_top_level_tests_module_is_one_pytest_collects` -- makes the shape impossible to reintroduce: every top-level `tests/*.py` must match one of pytest's default `python_files` patterns or be `conftest.py`. **Red on exactly those three files when written**, green after the deletions. A module under `tests/` that pytest never collects reads as coverage and is not.

  **Per file, the measurements.** None of the three was collected: `pytest.ini` names `testpaths = tests` and no `python_files`, so pytest's default `test_*.py` / `*_test.py` applied and none of the three names matched (`pytest --collect-only` over the full suite mentioned `profile_memory` zero times). None could import: all three `import psutil` at module scope and `psutil` is in no `setup.py` list and not installed in the contributor venv, so pointing pytest at any of them stopped at `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'psutil'`. `profile_memory.py` asserted `maxtasksperchild == 10` against the `25` `_run_export_batch` has passed for releases -- it would have gone red on its first assertion had it ever run -- and despite its name contains no memory profiling at all; its own docstring says it "mocks the structure". The two that do profile, `detect_memory_leak.py` and `profile_export_memory.py`, are broken against today's API: run with `psutil` stubbed, both print `ERROR: Export failed for temp_export_1mb.dcm: 'MockInstance' object has no attribute 'sop_class_uid'` from `_export_instance_worker`, swallow it, and conclude `Total Growth: 0.00 MB` and `Estimated Memory Cost Per Worker: 0.00 MB`. A profiler that measures nothing and prints a figure is #347's defect class one directory over. None of the three has been touched since the project rename (#62); no collected test, workflow, doc or script imports or names them (the two mentions are in dated records under `docs/superpowers/`, left alone: neither is a clause the deletion falsifies).

  **Why the two files the issue does not name are in this entry.** The collection contract cannot exist while they do, and a carve-out list for them would be the silent-skip pattern this tree keeps writing down (#162). The #335 scope argument -- a second fix landing quietly inside another issue's change-set is a change nobody reviewed -- is met by naming all three here, in the change message and in the PR, each with the measurement that justifies it. **Rejected:** the issue's option 2, `psutil` in the `tests` extra and a rename so CI runs it -- a dependency for zero working tests. **Rejected:** the issue's option 3 as written, relocating the profilers to `tests/benchmarks/` -- there is no working memory profiling to move, and `python -m tests.benchmarks.profile_export_memory` would be a documented entry point that prints `0.00 MB` on a swallowed error. A working export memory profiler is a feature and is filed separately rather than built here. **Rejected:** fixing the `10` and leaving the file uncollected -- the issue's own option 1, and the trap re-armed.

  **The guard's shape.** The top-level `tests/*.py` glob intersected with what `git ls-files tests` tracks when git can answer (an untracked scratch module must not turn CI red -- #324's argument; a file added but not yet tracked is invisible, which is correct because CI starts from a clean tree; no git means the bare glob, never a skip). Top level only, and that is a statement about the directory's contents rather than about location: `tests/benchmarks/` holds `python -m` entry points by design, but a `tests/benchmarks/test_foo.py` *would* be collected since `testpaths` recurses, so the test does not claim benchmarks are uncollectable. It asserts `pytest.ini` has no non-comment `python_files` line (`^\s*python_files\s*=`), because the default patterns are the premise -- widening them to `*.py` would make every offender collectable and the test green while changing what the suite runs -- and floors at 150 collectable modules (195 today) so a broken sweep cannot pass vacuously -- a floor deliberately far under the count, because every branch that adds a test file moves it and a pin would make that a merge conflict. Neighbouring floors after the deletions, measured on the branch as merged: the #292 escape sweep compiles 245 files against its `> 200` floor (247 on `main` immediately before this branch: minus three deletions, plus `tests/test_redaction_worker_count.py`), and the sdist test-suite check sees 196 top-level `tests/*.py` (198 before). Neither floor is moved.

## [0.9.2] - 2026-09-05

### Breaking

- **`session.export()` can say it wrote nothing: it returns an `ExportSummary`, and raises `ExportError` when zero of N planned instances reached disk (#191).** New `io_handlers.ExportError`, exported as `isocenter.ExportError`. `_export_dicom` returns `io_handlers.ExportSummary` on every path, including its empty-plan early return. **Breaking**, and the exact shape is below.

  **What a previously-working call now does.** `session.export(folder)` returned `None`. A run that delivered all three of its files and a run that delivered none were indistinguishable at the call site: the failures were audited by #181 and graded by the compliance report, and the *call* looked identical either way. `export()` now returns a summary, and when **zero of N planned instances were written and at least one failed** it raises `io_handlers.ExportError` -- a `RuntimeError` subclass carrying `.failures` (`[(entity_uid, details)]`) and `.attempted`. A caller who wrote `session.export(out)` and read nothing back is unaffected on a successful or partial export, and now gets an exception on a total one.

  **The raise is last**, after all five records the run produces: the collision report, the recoverable-identity disclosure, the `_last_export_written`/`_last_export_requested` pair (#181), the `EXPORT` audit row (#166, which the report's export boundary keys on -- #153) and `Done.`. Same order `_apply_redaction_rules` uses for `RedactionError`, for the same reason: a caller who catches it still holds a correct graph, a complete audit trail, and a report grading `REVIEW_REQUIRED` with `Instances Written | 0 of 3 requested`. A test asserts all five survive the raise.

  **Rejected: raising on any failure.** A partial export is a real, usable result; raising would discard the summary naming which files landed and would have to decide the fate of files already on disk. **Rejected: leaving it returning `None`** -- that is the defect restated. **Rejected: changing the WFDB exporter to match** -- #191 scopes it out, its `List[str]` is consumed positionally by ~25 call sites, and `[]` versus `None` already lets a caller detect that nothing was written. `Exporter.export`'s base docstring now says the return is the format's own result object and that every format's must allow that detection; its `-> List[str]` annotation is dropped, because it was a promise the registry cannot keep -- and `DicomFormatExporter.export`'s is dropped with it, since the concrete adapter restating the base class's wrong promise one layer down is the same falsehood in a place a reader is likelier to look.

  **Zero of zero does not raise.** An empty plan returns `ExportSummary()`: a subset that matched nothing is not a failed export, and the `EXPORT` row above that early return already says so. The guard is `written == 0 **and** failures`.

  `ExportSummary` becomes public API, so one subtlety is now user-visible prose rather than an internal note: `written` counts **de-duplicated** UIDs, because the UID names the output file -- two instances sharing one are two successful write operations and one file, the second having overwritten the first (#197).

  `write_tree`'s bare `RuntimeError` is deliberately **left alone**: it and `ExportError` describe different behaviours -- "this serializer could not write" and "the pipeline delivered nothing" -- and changing it would be a second API-shape change riding on the authorised one. `ExportError` subclasses `RuntimeError` so one `except RuntimeError` still catches both; `tests/test_api_coherence.py` gains a **new** test for that (the existing tree-equality test pins layout and is untouched, so a failure contract folded into it would make one red mean two things).

  One existing expectation flips and is updated with its reason in place: `tests/test_export_failure_audit.py`'s `filesystem` arm fails every write, so `_run` now catches `ExportError` -- the helper's subject is what survives the failure, and the raise happens after all of it. Its `validator` arm breaks one of three, is a partial export, and still does not raise.

### Changed

- **`session.export()` runs in processes by decision, and now says so when it overrides a request for threads (#185).** One warning arm in `parallel._use_threads`; docstring prose there and on `Session._run_export_batch`; two rows in `docs/environment.md`; three tests in `tests/test_parallel_contract.py`. **No behaviour change to the strategy**: `_use_threads` returns exactly what it returned on every path, and the nine test files that rest on processes-on-export are untouched.

  `_run_export_batch` passes `maxtasksperchild=25`, and `_use_threads` answers recycling first and unconditionally, because only `multiprocessing.Pool` implements it. So the heaviest path in the library -- the one that pickles an `ExportContext` per instance, attributes, sequences and, where pixels are resident, a numpy array, across a pipe -- takes the process path on **every** interpreter, including a free-threaded one, where every other `run_parallel` call site takes threads. `docs/environment.md` documented `ISOCENTER_FORCE_THREADS` as the way to force threads, and on the export path it did nothing, silently.

  **The decision: keep processes.** The recycling is not decorative. A leak in a JPEG 2000 encoder on a 100GB+ run is a real thing to defend against, and a thread pool has no equivalent -- there is no process to recycle. The trade is leaked C-library memory against the cost of pickling every task, and it is taken in favour of the memory: an export that finishes slowly is better than one that is OOM-killed at hour six. The two alternatives #185 records were weighed and not taken -- dropping the recycling on free-threaded builds only, which accepts unreclaimable leaked memory on exactly the interpreter this project is adding support for, and making it conditional on `use_compression`, which makes the memory behaviour of a run depend on an export option most callers never set.

  **What changes is the silence.** `_use_threads` now warns when, and only when, a thread request was actually contradicted -- `force_threads=True` or `ISOCENTER_FORCE_THREADS=1` **and** a `maxtasksperchild`. The message names both levers, quotes the recycling value, says `session.export()` always sets it, and says which lever to unset. It is in `_use_threads` and nowhere else because that function *is* the precedence, `_resolve_strategy` calls it once per `run_parallel`, and it runs in the parent where the caller's logger is reachable. On the ordinary export path -- no environment variable, no argument -- it is silent, and a test asserts that silence: a warning on every export would be noise that teaches readers to filter this logger. That test `delenv`s `ISOCENTER_FORCE_THREADS` -- review caught it reading the ambient environment, where it was asserting silence about whatever the operator happened to have exported and staying green inside a full run only because a sibling test's `setenv` is undone after it. Confirmed: with the variable exported, `_use_threads(False, 25)` emits exactly the warning the test claims is absent. A test whose subject is "no warning" must own every input that could produce one.

  **With both `ISOCENTER_FORCE_THREADS` and `ISOCENTER_MAX_TASKS_PER_CHILD` set, every `run_parallel` call warns**, not only export -- ingest, the PHI scan, OCR verification, zone discovery, redaction. That is correct, since the operator asked for two contradictory things at every call site, and it is why the message names the lever to unset rather than only reporting that a conflict exists.

  **The prose is pinned by a characterization test, not by a grep.** A prose change admits no red, and grepping `docs/environment.md` for the new sentences would pin their wording and pass just as happily if the wording were wrong. `test_export_runs_in_processes_by_decision` captures the kwargs `_run_export_batch` passes and asserts `maxtasksperchild == 25` -- and then asserts the warning's own sentence quotes *that captured number*, not a second literal `25`. The message is prose in shipped log output that repeats a value nothing reads from the call, which is exactly how `tests/profile_memory.py`'s `10` drifted (#347); verified by moving the export call to `50` and updating the kwarg assertion with it, which leaves the log line telling operators `25` and this assertion red. its docstring records what that holds still and names the eight test files plus `tests/profile_memory.py` that assume the subprocess boundary and would have to be revisited before it became `None`. Review caught that the ninth is listed for its assumption rather than its protection -- it is neither collected nor importable, and its own `maxtasksperchild` assertion has drifted to `10` against the shipped `25`; both docstrings now say so and point at #347 rather than lending it authority it does not have.

  **`docs/environment.md`, two rows.** `ISOCENTER_FORCE_THREADS` now states that it does not apply to `session.export()`, that the export path is processes on every interpreter including free-threaded builds, why, and that the request is warned about rather than dropped -- including the practical consequence the issue's comment names: `export()` is the one path that cannot be debugged, breakpointed or coverage-measured in the calling process, and there is no `ISOCENTER_MAX_WORKERS=1` escape hatch either, because `run_parallel` has no in-process path. `ISOCENTER_MAX_TASKS_PER_CHILD` now states that it cannot reach the export path in either direction, since `_resolve_strategy` consults the environment only when the argument is `None`.

  **Free-threaded behaviour is reasoned from source and left to CI.** Only 3.14.6 with the GIL enabled was run here. The change adds a log record and alters no return value on any path, so the 3.14t gate is the check.

- **`FLATTENED_PAGE_SIZE` stops advertising a knob it never provided, and a bad `page_size` reads as a bad argument (#202).** One constant renamed to `SqliteStore._FLATTENED_PAGE_SIZE`, one default argument and one docstring following it, one widened guard in `get_flattened_instances` (`isocenter/persistence.py`); three tests in `tests/test_dataframe_export.py`. **The public name is deleted, not aliased.**

  `SqliteStore.FLATTENED_PAGE_SIZE = 500` was a public class attribute, and `get_flattened_instances` took its default from it. A default argument is evaluated once, when the `def` runs, so the `500` was baked into `__defaults__` at import and the attribute was never read again: rebinding it -- on the class, on an instance, or on a subclass -- did nothing. Measured: after `SqliteStore.FLATTENED_PAGE_SIZE = 2`, a default-argument walk over six rows took **one** connection, where honouring the `2` would have taken three; an explicit `page_size=2` took four. Two things pointed a user at it as though it were configuration: the docstring named it, and the nine-line comment beside it explains a trade-off that only matters if someone might change it. The rendered API reference was **not** one of them -- an earlier draft of this entry said it was, and the correction is below. Two spellings for one behaviour with only one of them working, failing silently: a user bounding memory on a large export got 500-row pages and no error.

  **Made private rather than made real, and there is no compatibility alias.** `page_size=` already is the one spelling for the behaviour, so making the attribute genuinely overridable would have added a second one rather than fixing the count. The comment stays -- it explains where 500 comes from -- and gains a sentence saying explicitly that this is the default and not a knob, which the underscore alone does not tell a reader. Pre-1.0, a renamed name is deleted, so `FLATTENED_PAGE_SIZE = _FLATTENED_PAGE_SIZE` is not added; a test asserts the public name is *absent*, because re-adding it for compatibility would restore exactly the two spellings that caused this.

  **Three exception cells change, and one of them changes when it fires.** The guard was `if page_size < 1`, which admits anything comparable to an int:

  | `page_size` | before | now |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `0`, `-1` | `ValueError` at the call | unchanged |
  | `None` | `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'int'` | `ValueError` |
  | `"5"` | `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'` | `ValueError` |
  | `2.5` | passed the guard; `sqlite3.IntegrityError: datatype mismatch` from `LIMIT ?` **on the first `next()`** | `ValueError` at the call |
  | `1e9` | passed the guard; same `IntegrityError` on the first `next()` | `ValueError` |
  | `True` | passed the guard and paged **one row at a time** | `ValueError` |

  None of these "worked", so nothing that was correct changes. The float rows are the ones worth the entry: the method is a plain function wrapping a generator *precisely* so its checks fire at the call rather than on the first `next()`, and a float gave that up -- it returned a generator, and the failure arrived a page later, as a database error out of a public method, for what is a caller's typo.

  **`bool` is refused before `int`, and the ordering is the mechanism.** `isinstance(True, int)` is `True` and `True < 1` is `False`, so `page_size=True` passed the old guard *and* would pass a naive `isinstance(page_size, int)` one -- and then page the walk one row at a time, silently and correctly, which is worse than an error. This repo refuses `bool` before `int` twice already for the same subclass reason: `_fallback_encoding`'s `bool` arm and `_value_fits_vr`'s ordering (#283), both with comments saying the ordering is what does the work. The comment here points at that precedent.

  **No `int()` coercion for a float**, deliberately: `1e9` is a whole number and `2.5` is not, and a rule that accepted the first would have to decide about the second. Refusing the type says which spelling the method takes, and the comment says so before someone adds the coercion "helpfully".

  **`_iter_flattened_instances` gets no guard of its own.** It is private and reachable only through the checked entry point; that division is the reason the wrapper exists and its docstring already explains it.

  **`docs/api/persistence.md` is left as a bare `::: isocenter.persistence`, and the docs reasoning this entry first carried was wrong in both directions.** It is corrected here rather than quietly dropped, because the wrong version is the one a reader would have reasoned from. Measured against the built site and against the live published page (`origin/gh-pages:api/persistence/index.html`):

  - **The stated harm never happened.** The published page carries 33 member anchors, every one of them a method or a dunder. No class attribute renders at all -- not `FLATTENED_PAGE_SIZE`, and not `SCHEMA` either. mkdocstrings documents an attribute only when it carries a docstring, and a `#:` comment is not one as far as griffe is concerned.
